#7791. Firm partners in Silicon Valley paid more than NY partners, new survey shows

In a reversal that could reflect the artificial intelligence-fueled technology industry boom, law firm partners in Silicon Valley earned more on average than partners in New York last year, according to a new survey. (Image from Shutterstock)

In a reversal that could reflect the artificial intelligence-fueled technology industry boom, law firm partners in Silicon Valley earned more on average than partners in New York last year, according to a new survey.

Compensation for Silicon Valley partners was $2.57 million on average in ​2025, 4% more than partners in New York, according to a survey of large firms.

The survey was released this week by legal recruiting agency Major, Lindsey & Africa and included more than 1,000 respondents, according to a story by Reuters.

Average partner compensation throughout the top 200 largest U.S. firms increased 10% to $1.55 million since 2024. In 2016, ​the figure was $877,000.

The survey also revealed that average hourly billing rate increased by 11%, from $1,114 in ⁠2024 to $1,242, according to Reuters.

#7790. Assessing the first round of oral arguments of the 2026-27 term

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson – typically the court’s most frequent speaker at oral argument – began the term relatively quietly. In Suncor Energy v. Boulder County, the first argued case, she spoke the fourth-most among the participating justices, accounting for only 12.1% of the court’s words. But that relative silence did not last. Jackson led three of the next four arguments and finished the six-case sitting with 6,254 words, significantly more than any of her colleagues.

The arguments produced other patterns, some less predictable. Jackson and Justice Sonia Sotomayor repeatedly concentrated their attention on the same litigating side, but Justice Neil Gorsuch did so as well, despite the justices’ ideological differences. At the same time, their questions did not necessarily point toward identical legal outcomes.

The cases themselves – and how they were treated – revealed something more. Disputes concerning climate litigation, veterans’ constitutional claims, retirement-plan investments, and environmental review all raised questions about when, where, and under what conditions judicial intervention is available. Indeed, that essentially became the theme of the court’s October session.

Jackson’s dominance and some unexpected cross-ideological alignment

As described above, Jackson’s relatively limited involvement in Suncor initially appeared to vary from one of the Supreme Court’s most consistent recent patterns. During the 2025-26 term, she accounted for 22% of justices’ total speech and led in 41 of 58 oral arguments. Yet in the first argument of this term, her 829 words represented only 12.1% of substantive justice speech, placing her fourth among eight participating justices. Across the other five arguments, however, Jackson’s share averaged 21.0%. By the end of the sitting, Jackson had spoken 6,254 words, more than any colleague, and accounted for 19.3% of all substantive justice speech.

Jackson’s questioning also revealed a recurring alignment with Sotomayor and, more surprisingly, Gorsuch. Across several disputes, the three justices repeatedly directed a disproportionate amount of attention toward the same side.

In Johnson v. United States Congress, for instance, Gorsuch questioned whether the veterans’ benefits system possessed the competence to adjudicate constitutional challenges, while Sotomayor emphasized the burden of forcing veterans through an administrative process prior to obtaining constitutional review. Jackson similarly challenged the government’s account of how constitutional questions were handled in practice. The three justices’ approaches differed, but all three explored weaknesses in the government’s proposed review scheme.

In Suncor, the justices’ shared focus covered up larger doctrinal disagreements. Jackson questioned whether the case was sufficiently developed for Supreme Court intervention. Sotomayor asked about the courts’ authority and whether specific arguments had been preserved. Gorsuch explored how the Clean Air Act affected federal common law and potential state-law restrictions.

These alignments should not be conflated with emerging voting coalitions, however. In Beaird v. United States, for example, a Federal Sentencing Guidelines case, Jackson and Gorsuch proved the argument’s two dominant speakers while developing substantially different accounts of the U.S. Sentencing Commission’s authority.

The lesson is this: The justices who identify pressure points in an argument do not always group along familiar ideological lines, and agreement about which position deserves examination need not produce agreement about the possible controlling rule.

Jackson’s individual prominence did not translate into liberal dominance of the court’s collective conversation. Across the six arguments, conservative justices contributed 54.3% of substantive justice speech, compared with 45.7% from the three liberals. Conservatives supplied the majority of justices’ words in five of the six cases, with Johnson the exception. This represents a somewhat different balance (so far) from the 50.9% conservative–49.1% liberal division reported in a previous Legalytics analysis of the 2025-26 term.

Perhaps more revealing was the distribution of participation within those blocs. Justice Brett Kavanaugh finished second across the sitting with 5,031 words, followed closely by Justice Elena Kagan (4,998) and Gorsuch (4,920). Yet the three justices occupied markedly different positions from argument to argument. Kavanaugh supplied 23.7% of the justice’ speech in Suncor but only 6.0% in Johnson. Gorsuch ranged from 25.7% in Beaird to just 1.2% in Salazar v. Paramount Global. Kagan, who averaged 21.2% across the opening-day arguments, averaged only 13.6% across the next four.

Overall, the six arguments revealed neither the conservative or liberal bloc dominating the conversation. Instead, participation shifted substantially with the legal questions presented, often placing different justices at the forefront of particular disputes. Those changes become especially consequential when examining the competing theories of judicial review and interpretive authority developed throughout the individual arguments.

Four arguments about access to judicial review

Four of the court’s first six arguments presented different versions of a recurring question: what must happen before a federal court can intervene in a case? The doctrines varied considerably, from Supreme Court jurisdiction and veterans’ constitutional claims to pleading requirements and administrative finality. Nevertheless, each argument required the justices to consider how procedural and institutional/justiciable boundaries determine whether a legal challenge can proceed.

The sharpest illustration came in Department of the Air Force v. Prutehi Guåhan, where the justices examined whether the Air Force’s decision to seek a territorial hazardous-waste permit constituted final federal agency action, and how that determination interacted with environmental review under a federal statute. The government received 67% of explicit question marks but accounted for only 52.7% of advocate speech. Its counsel, Sopan Joshi, experienced a 60% cutoff rate, which was the highest among the 15 advocates appearing during the sitting.

The exchanges revealed different understandings of when an agency decision is settled enough to justify judicial intervention. Kagan questioned whether an agency’s completed deliberations could be rendered non-final simply because another regulator’s approval remained necessary. Jackson, typically on Kagan’s side, focused on the opposite possibility: if Guam’s permitting authority could impose conditions materially changing the Air Force’s project, perhaps the application remained a proposal rather than an operative federal commitment. Justices Clarence Thomas and Amy Coney Barrett called out the unusual institutional arrangement, with the federal government appearing as a regulated applicant rather than the permitting authority itself.

Gorsuch and Chief Justice John Roberts approached the problem from another angle, exploring whether postponing review could leave challengers without an effective opportunity to challengee the federal government’s environmental obligations. Kavanaugh explored the practical consequences of requiring successive rounds of review.

The relationship to the opening-day cases is telling. In Suncor, Thomas and Jackson questioned whether the dispute was sufficiently developed for Supreme Court review, particularly with other federal issues and several factual questions still unresolved below. In Johnson, the justices confronted a very different institutional barrier: whether constitutional challenges involving veterans’ benefits must proceed through the specialized administrative-review system rather than federal district court. Jackson, Sotomayor, and Gorsuch each tested aspects of the government’s proposed route, including whether it provided a practical means of resolving constitutional claims.

Anderson v. Intel Corporation Investment Policy Committee brought up a related yet distinct procedural issue. There, the question was what a retirement-plan plaintiff must allege to advance a claim that an ERISA fiduciary failed to use the requisite “care, skill, prudence, or diligence” under certain circumstances. Kavanaugh and Jackson distinguished underperforming investments from allegedly imprudent asset-allocation strategies, while Kagan and Barrett examined how rigorous a “meaningful investment benchmark” must be.

These cases do not rest on a particular judicial ideology. But they all deal with the availability of judicial review: whether the litigation has reached a proper point, the question of an adequate forum, the sufficiency of the allegations, and whether the court’s intervention is appropriate yet.

Beaird: competing theories of legal authority

No argument during the sitting generated more speech from the justices than Beaird v. United States. The justices contributed 7,791 words, more than twice their total in Anderson, with Gorsuch and Jackson accounting for 25.7% and 22.4% of these, respectively. Together, the two justices provided nearly half the court’s substantive speech. Yet their exchanges revealed a profound difference in how they understood the authority of the U.S. Sentencing Commission and the legal status of its commentary.

The dispute asks whether Stinson v. United States, the court’s 1993 decision requiring deference to Sentencing Guidelines commentary under specified conditions, continues to supply the governing rule. The case’s unusual alignment further distinguished the argument. Both Beaird and the United States supported vacating the judgment, and the court thus appointed a “friend of the court,” Anthony Dick, to defend Stinson. The petitioner-aligned advocates consequently accounted for 68.3% of advocate speech and received 80.1% of justice words. This imbalance partly reflects the unusual distribution of advocates rather than necessarily indicating hostility toward their position.

Jackson, who once served on the Sentencing Commission, began by challenging the premise that the Sentencing Guidelines and their commentary can meaningfully be separated. In her account, sentencing judges rely on both parts of the Guidelines Manual to calculate the recommended sentencing range. Commentary helps determine how provisions operate together as opposed to consisting of an unrelated agency interpretation. She returned to Congress’ decision to establish a sentencing framework intended to limit disparities among similarly situated defendants, questioning whether importing limitations from administrative deference doctrine would undermine that design.

Gorsuch’s questioning approached the problem from a very different institutional perspective. He examined where Congress expressly authorized binding commentary, why the Commission should be able to accomplish through commentary what it could instead accomplish through formal Guidelines amendments, and whether deference would weaken the procedural safeguards associated with that process. His concerns extended to the incentives created by allowing the Commission to make authoritative interpretations without necessarily following the same procedures applicable to the Guidelines themselves.

Other justices explored possible consequences of either approach. Kavanaugh repeatedly returned to the stability of a system operating under Stinson for more than three decades, questioning whether revisiting the doctrine might introduce new uncertainty into sentencing. Kagan examined whether Congress’ express recognition of policy statements complicated efforts to distinguish them from commentary, suggesting that differences in terminology might not fully resolve the question of authority.

The exchanges suggest several possible routes to a decision: reaffirming the current system, limiting the circumstances under which commentary receives controlling weight, or requiring a more explicit statutory basis for binding interpretations. They also illustrate a theme from earlier research on the relationship between oral argument and eventual opinions: The most revealing material may not be which advocate received the most questions, but the competing legal frameworks the justices developed as they questioned counsel.

The first six arguments also revealed substantial differences in how advocates were able to develop their answers. Across 982 advocate speaking turns, 420 ended in an explicitly identifiable cutoff by a justice, a rate of 42.8%. That figure was somewhat higher on the first day (45.2%) than during the four subsequent arguments (41.4%), but the variation among individual advocates was significantly larger.

Joshi, representing the Air Force in Prutehi, experienced the sitting’s highest cutoff rate at 60.0%, with 66 of his 110 turns ending that way. Kannon Shanmugam followed at 56.9% in Suncor, while Paul Clement was at 55.2% in Salazar. These were not merely differences between government and private counsel but arose in disputes involving separate statutes, procedural issues, and judicial argument coalitions.

Even advocates supporting the same position had different experiences. In Suncor, Shanmugam’s median response was 13.5 words, compared with 35 for Principal Deputy Solicitor General Sarah Harris, who supported the petitioner and experienced a 40.0% cutoff rate.

The differences illustrate how much the structure and subject of individual exchanges can shape an advocate’s opportunity to explain a legal position. These observations also complement earlier Empirical SCOTUS findings about an increasingly active oral-argument bench.

Jackson’s unusually limited participation in the first argument of the term, Suncor, proved to be an exception rather than the beginning of a broader retreat. Across six arguments, she remained the court’s leading individual speaker, even as the distribution of judicial participation shifted considerably from case to case.

More surprising was the relationship between the justices’ attention and their ideological positions. Jackson, Sotomayor, and Gorsuch consistently concentrated on the same litigating side. But their exchanges also revealed why common questioning should not be confused with voting the same. In Beaird, for example, Jackson and Gorsuch developed competing accounts of institutional authority despite both dominating the argument.

The substantive disputes supplied another connection. From Suncor and Johnson to Anderson and Prutehi, the justices repeatedly considered when judicial review should be available. Despite some of the substantive issues in play, the defining theme of this term’s start was one of judicial power.

Dr. Adam Feldman is the creator and author of the blog Empirical SCOTUS and the Substack Legalytics.

Recommended Citation: Adam Feldman, Assessing the first round of oral arguments of the 2026-27 term, SCOTUSblog (Oct. 27, 2026, 10:30 AM), https://www.scotusblog.com/2026/10/assessing-the-first-round-of-oral-arguments-of-the-2026-27-term/

#7789. We Are Underlings

In line with my belief that it’s important to always keep the resumé fresh, I signed up for first aid training six months ago and the first class is today. The Nine Circles exalts dying and death, but not for guests. Plus, most of us sit for nine hours a day and eat greasy meals at lunch, putting us at risk for croaking in our cubicles. A knowledge of first aid does not help me do my back-of-house job better, though if a colleague has a heart attack at work, I’ll be able to perform cpr while waiting for the paramedics to arrive. Even though we’ll be taking an exam during the final class, I’m treating these training sessions as a vacation from my desk. The best part is that Charles and Charlotte are also taking the course; he’s doing it because he cares about the welfare of other employees and she’s doing it because she’ll be on park grounds from time to time working on the new attractions.

Three months ago, Human Resources sorted everyone with a Chinese surname into the Cantonese training sessions without first checking whether we could read or write the language. HR’s mandate seems to be cart before horse. Although it was embarrassing to admit that I was illiterate except for menus and select street signs, I reported that my understanding of body part names and medical terminology was limited to English. (What’s the word for spleen in Cantonese? I still don’t know.) Human Resources Associate Gallant Sum instructed me to take the course on evenings and weekends at a community centre with our expat colleagues—the Nine Circles would still pay the fees, he assured me, but the company would not consider these thirty hours as overtime. But then it turned out that the executive team wanted some of the bilingual Hong Kong staff members to take the course in English to better serve international guests and vips, so Human Resources had to scramble to implement these classes on top of the final push to hire an additional hundred people to round out the team.

Charles and Charlotte are already in the meeting room when I arrive at 9:12 a.m., the official start time at the Nine Circles.

“Is this an actual first aid training session or a mass firing?” Charlotte asks, as she scans the room to see which colleagues are present.

“My tour with Pamela Poon, Raymond Shek, and Jade Chen Church went pretty poorly yesterday, so I can imagine why I’d be fired,” I say.

“I’m sure it wasn’t as bad as you think,” Charlotte says.

“Well, I didn’t make any serial killer jokes this time,” I say. Then I’m relieved to spot the Secretary to the Head of Project Delivery. “Helen Chan’s here, and I don’t think they would fire any of the secretaries. Everything would come to a stop if even one was terminated.”

“She’s pretty essential to the park opening on time,” Charles says. “Remember when she went on vacation?” When Helen took her annual leave to get married and go on her honeymoon, the paperwork for the air filtration system for the Afterlife lab went missing and Project Delivery started construction without understanding that the omission of this system violated building code. Charlotte spotted the error and reported it to the executive team and managerial staff. She noted that without air filtration it would be unsafe to display some of our most famous corpses. No one listened to her because she’s not head of her department. The Chaplins and I discovered, during an investigation that we conducted on our own time, that a Project Delivery manager had buried the paperwork to save money, but his gamble resulted in a million-dollar mistake. For reasons unknown, that manager still has a job at the Nine Circles, and somehow Helen got written up for this incident despite eight underlings reporting to the executive team that it was not her fault.

I have one of the jobs that is considered nonessential. I don’t fetch coffee or set up conference calls or schedule important meetings or handle corpses.

What I don’t say is that out of everyone in the training room, most of whom are junior staff from Administration, I have one of the jobs that is considered nonessential. I don’t fetch coffee or set up conference calls or schedule important meetings or handle corpses. No one up on aside from the Executive Director seems to understand that marketing is necessary to get paying guests through the turnstiles. Mirabella Lam, Educational Programmes Manager, believes that the high quality of her programming is enough to draw a crowd and insists that trying to attract attention is crass.

“But how will the public know about your projects if we don’t spread the word?” I once asked Mirabella during an all-team meeting. “We do good work,” she said, directing her comment toward the Executive Director. The ceo, Dalton Northcott, was not in attendance that day, or Mirabella would have addressed him instead. One can sum up Mirabella’s work philosophy as “managing up.” I later discovered I’d made a sworn enemy with my well-meaning query. Mirabella is employee ten, so even though she doesn’t outrank most of us in terms of the org chart, she wields her seniority as a sort of authority.

Many underlings have never met the ceo. With his travel schedule, he’s rarely at the Hong Kong offices. Early on, when the team was smaller, I met Dalton at the groundbreaking ceremony and asked him how to keep my houseplants alive—I’d read that he had a PhD in botany and an impressive orchid collection. His response was warm and engaging, yet I could sense he had boundaries in place that prevented the interaction from becoming overfamiliar. This gave me a false sense of safety—I believed the ceo was a leader I could trust.

The first aid teacher arrives and does not introduce himself. Instead, he says, “Where are we going to eat lunch?” Then he wipes his sweaty forehead with a faded pink towel.

There’s a ten-second silence that feels like an eternity. Many of the participants in this training session are under twenty-five and are too shy to make eye contact when they do their rounds with the mail or set up a projector for meetings. There is no way any of us are going to give up our lunch hour of rest (or work catch-up) to entertain our first aid teacher, but we have to figure out a diplomatic way to communicate this information.

“Most of us brought our lunches,” says Charlotte.

“There’s a food court downstairs in the mall, as well as a supermarket,” I say. We were supposed to have moved into the offices built on park grounds six months ago, but the sprinkler system keeps going off and no one can figure out how to fix it, so now they’re pulling out the entire thing and reinstalling it and most of us are still in our rented office space in the mall. On the way in every morning, I pass Celine, Chanel, and Louis Vuitton and see the salespeople lovingly dusting handbags that cost more than my monthly salary.

The teacher looks disappointed. Did he imagine we’d want to discuss the finer points of guts and gore while eating dumplings? When it’s clear no one is going to invite him to lunch, he opens his PowerPoint presentation. The first slide features a grainy black-and-white scan from a newspaper.

“What’s happening here?” he shouts. None of us can figure out what’s depicted in the image.

The blobs could be a cat playing the piano. “Come on!” he says. “What would you do if you came across this accident?”

“The photo is a bit on the blurry side,” says Charles, ever polite.

“Common sense! First thing at a scene, no illegal touch!” says the teacher.

I wonder if he’s had complaints against him while administering cpr. I don’t remember any instruction about illegal touch from my previous first aid training sessions in Canada. Icarus Sun from Administration, whose clothes always look shrunken in a cool streetwear way, is taking notes. I wonder if he’s writing Do not molest the injured person.

The room is airless, making me sluggish. I yawn and unzip my jacket. “Wah,” says the teacher, switching to Cantonese. His eyes are on my tits. “I thought you were going to take it all off.”

I zip my jacket back up. Charlotte and I look at each other. “What a perv,” she whispers. No one else in the room seems to have noticed what has happened, not even the Human Resources Associate who is observing the session to ensure everything goes smoothly, so I let it pass. “In a few weeks, I will introduce you to a beautiful lady for cpr,” the teacher says. “Her name is Annie.” Icarus is still taking notes. CPR on beautiful lady! “But what’s going on in the slide?” asks Charlotte.

“You will understand when you meet the beautiful lady!” the first aid teacher says with a wide smile on his face. As the minutes pass like snails trying to cross a freeway during rush hour, I think about all the unanswered emails in my inbox and slip into a dissociative state.

#7787. Debra Webb and Allison Brennan on villains, suspense, and writing standalone thrillers

USA Today Bestselling author Debra Webb began her career writing romantic suspense but by the early 2000s had started to lean into darker suspense. A few years later she was fully immersed in the world of thrillers. It was at the very first International Thriller Writers conference in Phoenix, Arizona where she met Allison Brennan.

Flash forward twenty years and Debra’s first standalone thriller, The Woman I’ve Become, is slated for October of this year. Longtime friend and fellow author Allison Brennan was one of the first to read the upcoming release and called it a “page-turning thriller!”

New York Times Bestselling author Allison Brennan also began her career writing romantic suspense for Ballantine Books, but in 2011 launched the Lucy Kincaid FBI thriller series. Now she has two series—the Quinn & Costa FBI thrillers, and the Angelhart Investigations PI series—and writes the occasional stand alone. Whisper Creek is her third standalone thriller, out in June. Allison is thrilled that the amazing Debra Webb is stepping into the standalone world.

Allison Brennan: I can’t believe it’s been twenty years. Twenty! Talk about feeling my age.

Debra Webb: No kidding! But I have to say it has been an amazing ride! The best part is we’re both still doing what we love–writing books!

AB: I absolutely loved The Woman I’ve Become. I honestly didn’t realize it was your first standalone! You’ve written a gazillion books. Haha. Why this one? What gave you that itch to write this book with this heroine?

DW: Thank you so much. It was time to do something different. I’ve always written stories with an eye toward what comes next for these characters. I love working with a large cast of characters, providing lots of options for moving forward with the next chapter in one or the other’s life.

DW: But when this story idea first sprouted, it was all about this one woman and the secrets she used like stones to build a life. As the story developed it became about how the story would end. How you battle your demons when they find you and they always do. Really, at its core this one is about survival and how this story would end. In fact, that was the working title, How This Ends.

I’m of the opinion that characters are the heart of our stories, yours and mine. Your newest release, Whisper Creek, is a perfect example of characters being the heart of a very twisted drama! What creative spark brought these characters into such a twisted and dangerous situation. I love, by the way, how you developed two distinct threats!

AB: Story is ultimately about character. Without character, it’s just a cool plot. The people make it a story worth reading.

AB: I’m sure you know this better than most writers, but writing isn’t easy. No book is “easy” to write. But some books are easier than others, where the story flows chapter by chapter and you, as the author, are whisked away while you write. For me, that book is Whisper Creek. While I had to do a lot of research about farming, northeast Texas, and storms, the story itself practically wrote itself. As for the creative spark, it was basically just “what if”—what if the bad guys are caught in a storm and can’t get away? And while that is an important part of the plot, the story is really about the McKenna family trying to save the farm against both man and Mother Nature.

DW: Your readers are going to love it! Research is so important in what we do. Although we write fiction, it’s crucial that we get things right–or at least believable.

AB: Agreed! Though research is also my favorite form of procrastination, haha.

DW: The storm in your story is such a unique element. It’s difficult to fight Mother Nature lol. Perhaps even harder to outsmart her. Do you have a favorite element you’ve used to thrust your characters into the middle of danger?

AB: Whatever works for the story. In Whisper Creek, I needed a storm in an area that was prone to flooding. I needed my characters to be cut off from the outside world in a realistic way. The last “wilderness thriller” (that’s what my editor calls these books, where setting and weather are an integral part of the story) was set during a snow storm. The next (I’m writing now!) is set in the Bob Marshall Wilderness in Montana. Not during a storm, but it’s a rugged and unforgiving landscape. But I love any type of story where the danger is organic to the plot!

DW: Your “wilderness” thrillers do sound awesome! And yes, it’s always better if the danger is organic. In The Woman I’ve Become, I ushered the characters from the city, Manhattan, to the place where the trouble started so many years before—Westport, Connecticut. It was a homecoming of sorts. Going back to where it all began. Sometimes it’s the going back to that place where the damage was done that builds the tension and fear best. But it also increases the danger in this story because there is the element of isolation at the family lake house.

Primarily it felt right for the characters to face-off in the place where it all started. When a story “feels right” the flow is smoother. As you say no story is “easy” to write but it sure helps when it flows the way you had hoped!

AB: I don’t think “normal” people (i.e. – not writers!) understand when we say it “feels” right, LOL. But that’s exactly how I think as well! We know intuitively when the story is working and when it’s not. Here’s a question I get a lot and I never have a good answer. How do you know when a story will make a good series and when it is really a stand alone? How did you know with The Woman I’ve Become? I usually say, “It’s about the characters” but that doesn’t feel complete enough.

DW: Wow! What a great question and also a difficult one to answer. Again, I believe it’s in part the “feeling” of wanting or needing to continue with the element that makes the series whether it’s the setting or the characters (really, usually the characters). I’ve written lots of series.

One of my favorites is the Faces of Evil series. That one I knew right from the moment the spark came that it would be a series. When Julia and Wendy from The Woman I’ve Become started to speak to me, I knew their story would be a stand alone. I understood that whatever happened, I needed to finish this thing that began between them decades before. It felt, as we’ve discussed, right.

AB: We have to trust our guts. Most of my series I create as a series. Either a police procedural where readers often expect characters to grow over time. For the Quinn & Costa series, I wanted to take my core group but move them around the country so they didn’t investigate in one place. For my Angelhart series, I wanted to focus more on family (a family of P.I.s) so set the book in Phoenix. Again, it just felt right!

Plus, I think with standalones, the characters aren’t usually in a position to have multiple crimes or mysteries in their life. This one “thing” that is happening IS their mystery, if that makes sense.

DW: You are spot ont! Which leads to another point that folks who aren’t writers sometimes don’t understand. When we’re developing a story idea (whether born of a plot element or a character), the synopsis or plan for the story ALWAYS changes because, believe it or not, the characters take the lead.

With every story I’ve written, it starts out as the story I want to tell but about a hundred pages in it becomes the story the characters need to tell. There’s this connection to the characters you’ve created that takes over, don’t you think?

AB: Hundred percent. I have never stuck to a synopsis; I don’t plot. People often don’t believe me, but it’s true. Usually my synopsis is all backstory. I know where the characters are when the story starts and why, but everything after the inciting incident changes as I write. The story feels more organic and natural that way.

But mostly, it’s the only way I can write. After fifty-two books, I don’t really want to mess with that (mostly) works! And yes, I know you have twice as many books as me!

DW: Yes! We are alike in that! My synopsis is basically back story as well. I often wonder if the editor thinks “I don’t remember that from the synopsis.” The characters lead and that’s the best way to tell a story. Once you know those characters you can trust them completely. They know where they need to go!

AB: Yes, exactly! And I find that I have to edit the first hundred pages a lot more than the last three hundred when I’m done with my first draft.

DW: Same here! Getting back to the research, I sometimes wonder if you and I were perhaps cops or PIs in another life. We so love the police procedural aspect of our stories. I catch myself when watching television (series and the news) anticipating what the cops will do next.

AB: I have loved mysteries and cop shows from early childhood. I grew up on Trixie Belden and Nancy Drew and my mom and I would watch Hill Street Blues, she let me stay up late to watch it! I’ve done several ride alongs with local police, participated in the FBI citizens academy, toured Quantico, viewed an autopsy, and more.

Now I have people I can call when I need information (including my daughter, who is a Phoenix PD officer!) I’ve found when I’m writing my standalones, where there is no law enforcement or it’s on the edge of the story, that I have to really think more about what an average person without training would do in these situations.

DW: Those are amazing resources and certainly adds to the realistic feel of writing from the perspective of the police or a private investigator. We share the love of those childhood stories and some of the best cop shows ever! But we’re both also very good at creating villains. Those shoes are a little tougher to step into when writing depraved killers. How do you do your research for those characters?

AB: I have a workshop called “The Villain’s Journey” taken in part from Christopher Vogler’s “The Writer’s Journey.” Basically, the villain is the hero of his own journey. That means he has clear (even if he’s crazy) motivations, goals, and conflicts. Why is he the way he is?

And not all villains are depraved. Some just do bad things. I need to know WHY. Once I know that, I can write them. Also, I remember that (usually) not all villains are a hundred percent evil. There needs to be at least one redeeming characteristic, something that makes them more human to readers. But sometimes the evil villains are the most fun to write! LOL.

DW: Every writer should go to your workshop on Villains. It is so true that we have to remember that the villains are people too. And, as you say, not all are depraved. There are levels of evil and each villain must have a reason they are the way they are… one that made them who they are. That background and motivation is as important for the villain as it is for any other character.

And the redeeming characteristic is absolutely essential. The human side of a villain is what draws the reader to him or her even when they don’t want to be drawn. I love how perfectly you defined exactly how to create the perfect villain!

Which brings me to the “bad thing.” The incident, the reason the characters must do what they do. Where does your inspiration for that important story element come from?

AB: I have no idea. I’m not being flip! Usually there are several little ideas that come together that give me that AHA! moment. For the Quinn & Costa series, I wanted a mobile FBI unit loosely based on the real-life Evidence Response Team. I only knew one of the characters when I started, and Kara Quinn wasn’t supposed to be a series character, but took over book one. (Then I had to figure out how to have an LAPD detective on the team permanently!)

For Whisper Creek I knew there was going to be a storm, and I knew that there were bad guys trapped in the storm. I knew the mother of the ranch (a widow), but the four kids all sort of developed as I wrote them. And there was no grandma in the synopsis that I pitched my editor, but she really makes the book.

And I didn’t know that the cat who escaped the barn in the prologue would become such an important part of the story! Have you ever had characters who you didn’t think would be important become pivotal to one of your books?

DW: Like you, I can seldom explain where the trouble comes from in a story as I’m beginning. More often than not I have a character who is in a situation and I build from there: what happened before and what happens after. Occasionally I know, as I did, in part, with my Vera Boyett series. I knew there were human remains in the cave and that the two older sisters had put them there. All the rest came as I wrote the story.

And, yes, those characters, human or animal, who turn into stars are so fun. In The Woman I’ve Become it’s the lakehouse caretaker. She’s so feisty! She evolved into such a great character.

AB: She was absolutely one of my favorites! I’m so glad I got to read an early copy of The Woman I’ve Become.

DW: It really has been such a pleasure talking about writing with you, Allison. Before we go, I’d love to give readers a glimpse into our everyday lives. What’s an average day for you?

AB: My writing life has changed over the years. When my kids were little, I was actually far more productive. I knew I HAD to write when they were in school because once they got home we had sports, homework, theater, and all the stuff that comes with raising a big family. Now, my youngest is twenty-one and I have all the time in the world…so I tend to procrastinate, haha.

But, generally, I wake up around 5 in the morning, go for my morning walk, have coffee and play word games, then sit at my computer from about 7-8 to respond to email, post on social media, etc. Then I have breakfast, and by 9, I start writing. I try to get up to walk and stretch a couple of times, but often forget. By 4 I’m brain dead and call it quits, whether I’ve written 500 words or 5,000 words. I used to write at night, but I don’t have the bandwidth anymore. (Unless I am near the end of a book and am super excited…even now, I’ve been known to write into the wee hours of the morning once or twice a month!)

I also now have a grandson! I babysit him once a week, so that’s my “day off.”

What about you? How do you write and what has changed over the years?

DW: You are amazing! Had to say that! My writing life is similar to yours! And I agree that it was far more structured back when I had school age kiddos. These days I’m up between five and six (sometimes earlier if I’m excited to get started).

I don’t do anything except make coffee before writing. It’s easier for me if I don’t let the world in first. I just dive in and do all the other stuff, social media, emails, etc., later. I write until I reach the point I wanted to reach that day (sometimes a few pages, sometimes a whole chapter). Then I do all the other stuff that life requires.

I also do the fun stuff. You know how I love renovating houses and treasure hunting at junk stores. Nowadays I’m pretty big into gardening, flower and vegetable, and there are the goats and chickens. We moved to a little farm a few years ago. And I have lots of grandkids who I adore! I feel very fortunate to do what I love and to be surrounded by the people I love.

AB: I am totally jealous. That is my dream. I used to have chickens, and I will have my farm and get them back! (And I hope my kids get the hint that I want more grandkids! Ha.) My goal is before I’m sixty to have my farm, but I’ll give my kids a few more years for the babies. What’s next for you after this book?

DW: I am sure your beautiful children will be giving you lots of grandbabies in the future! Ah, what’s next? First, I will write as they say until they pry my cold, dead fingers from the keyboard! I’m working on a new cop series, Flynn & Beckett, for Thomas & Mercer and then comes my next standalone. Before we go, please tell us what’s coming next for you!

AB: I’m with you—I’ll always write. I can’t imagine retiring. I’m definitely looking forward to your new series! As far as what I’m doing…the third book in my Angelhart Investigations series, I’ll Be Watching You, came out in September, and the eighth book in my Quinn & Costa series, One Last Warning, is out in January!

I’m currently writing my next standalone, then I’ll jump into writing the next Quinn & Costa book. I also have a short story coming from Amazon Originals later this year, and a novella in the Quinn & Costa world late next year! I’m busy, but definitely no complaints.

DW: You are amazing, Allison. Be sure and drop by Allison’s website (allisonbrennan.com) for more about her books. I’d love you to drop by mine (debrawebb.com) and check out what’s new and coming soon. Thank you all so much for listening in to our conversation! Cheers!

Debra Webb is a USA Today bestselling author of more than 180 novels, including The Woman I've Become. She is the recipient of the prestigious Romantic Times Career Achievement Award for Romantic Suspense, as well as numerous Reviewers' Choice Awards. In 2012, Webb was honored as the first recipient of the esteemed L. A. Banks Warrior Woman Award for her courage, strength, and grace in the face of adversity. After publishing her hundredth novel, she also received the distinguished RWA Centennial Award. The author has sold more than ten million books in numerous languages and countries. Allison Brennan is the New York Times and USA Today bestselling author of over fifty novels, including the Lucy Kincaid and Max Revere series and the recent novel Whisper Creek. She was nominated for Best Paperback Original Thriller by the International Thriller Writers and is a two-time winner of the Daphne du Maurier Award by Kiss of Death.

#7786. A Ken Paxton Moment

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

As Texas AG, Paxton's done a lot of controversial and in-my-opinion unwise things, but this is the one that sticks in my craw

I have stayed away from discussing any of the many important electoral contests that will be (hopefully) decided today.  But given that he is at the center of one of the most hotly-contested Senate seats, I can't help being reminded of his conduct during the campaign to overturn the 2020 election results, and what may have been the lowest of many low points in Ken Paxton's career to date.

In December 2020, when he was Attorney General of Texas, Paxton was the attorney of record in a lawsuit against the states of Georgia, Michigan, Pennsylvania, and Wisconsin, seeking to overturn the 2020 election results in those states.  He petitioned the Supreme Court to exercise its original jurisdiction to hear the case, and to do so on an expedited basis. [See my blog posting at the time here; Paxton's papers filed at SCOTUS are posted here].

Expert analysis using a commonly accepted statistical test raises serious questions as to the integrity of this election. The probability of former Vice President Biden winning the popular vote in the four Defendant States—Georgia, Michigan, Pennsylvania, and Wisconsin—independently given President Trump's early lead in those States as of 3 a.m. on November 4, 2020, is less than one in a quadrillion, or 1 in 1,000,000,000,000,000. For former Vice President Biden to win these four States collectively, the odds decrease to less than one in a quadrillion to the fourth power (i.e., 1 in 1,000,000,000,000,000^4).

The same less than one in a quadrillion statistical improbability [applies to] Mr. Biden winning the popular vote in the four Defendant States. . . . Again, the statistical improbability of Mr. Biden winning the popular vote in these four States collectively is 1 in 1,000,000,000,000,000.

Put simply, there is substantial reason to doubt the voting results in the Defendant States.

Indeed there is!  Prima facie proof of fraud in the counting of ballots, I'd say. But only, of course, it it's correct, or at least close to correct. But it's not correct.  It is, as anyone with a knowledge of elementary statistics would have recognized immediately, simply and laughably wrong. The technical term is, I believe, "utter bullshit." I explain why here.  The probability that Joe Biden would end up with a majority in any of those is not one in a quadrillion - let alone one in a quadrillion to the 4th power (!), which is approximately equal to the probability that the sun will rise in the West tomorrow, and will have developed the capacity for human speech - nor anything close to one in a quadrillion.

Hey, we all make mistakes, right? What is most disgraceful about this episode is not that Paxton screwed up in his brief to the Court; it is that he never acknowledges his error, either publicly or, more importantly perhaps, to the Court. His assertion that the probability that Biden actually carried these States was equal to the probability that you would pick the single blue marble from a collection of 1,000,000,000,000,000 marbles, is a falsehood, and it is one that is at the core of his argument, in a case that was of grave importance to the future of the country. If Paxton didn't catch that falsehood before he filed his papers with the Court, he's merely a lousy lawyer, which I suppose is nothing to get too worked up about, given that there always will be plenty of lousy lawyers out there. But if he doesn't acknowledge that he has misled the Court after those misstatements are revealed - if he doesn't tell the Court that it has to ignore the part of his argument that relied on this incorrect understanding of statistics - then he's in a much more sinister category.

That this is the candidate whom the Texas Republican party chose as its candidate for U.S. Senate speaks volumes about the current state of the Rule of Law in this Administration. I'm sure that Mr. Paxton is looking forward, assuming the results go his way, to forging a close working relationship with Attorney General Todd Blanche, who is similarly scrupulous in his adherence to fundamental Rule of Law principles (as in the Slush Fund fraud-on-the-court perpetrated by Blanche and the DOJ].

David Post is currently an Adjunct Scholar at the Cato Institute, and was previously a professor at Beasley School of Law at Temple University.

#7785. Rivals race to rescue Weil Gotshal lawyers as firm heads toward closure

Several leading law firms are looking to take on junior lawyers and trainees from Weil, Gotshal & Manges after its management committee recommended an orderly wind-down of the firm’s global operations. (Photo from Shutterstock)

Several leading law firms are looking to take on junior lawyers and trainees from Weil, Gotshal & Manges after its management committee recommended an orderly wind-down of the firm’s global operations.

Law.com reported Thursday that Sullivan & Cromwell and Paul, Weiss, Rifkind, Wharton & Garrison are speaking with Weil Gotshal’s associates and trainees, and that other firms—including DLA Piper, Simpson Thacher & Bartlett and Latham & Watkins—have varying degrees of interest and engagement. According to Law.com, Weil Gotshal is working to find employment for as many people as possible.

Law.com further reported that priorities differ among the suitors. One source said Sullivan & Cromwell is currently favoring associates over partners, while another said Paul Weiss has already brought on several Weil Gotshal partners and is still courting junior lawyers. Meanwhile, another source told Law.com that some firms are offering places to prospective trainees who were due to join Weil Gotshal in September.

The wind-down still needs formal approval, with a partnership vote expected this week. Weil Gotshal’s leaders said the recommendation followed a thorough review of alternatives, and sources said partners have begun telling clients that the firm cannot continue. According to Law.com, the firms named were approached for comment.

#7784. Court declines to restore Biden-era regulation allowing some deportation proceedings to be suspended

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

The Supreme Court on Tuesday declined to restore a Biden-era regulation that allows immigration judges to suspend some deportation proceedings. In a brief, unsigned order, the court turned down a request from three cities and a group that provides legal services to immigrants to pause an agreement between Texas and the U.S. Department of Justice that threw out the rule.

The regulation at the center of the dispute, which provides what is known as “administrative closure,” was adopted by the Executive Office for Immigration Review, part of the Department of Justice, in 2024. Under it, immigration judges may suspend some deportation proceedings – for example, to allow a crime victim or witness to seek relief, such as asylum, from the U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services, which is a separate agency.

In June of this year, Texas went to federal court in Wichita Falls, where its case was assigned to Chief U.S. District Judge Reed O’Connor – the only federal judge in that area. Calling the administrative-closure rule “one part of the Biden-Harris Administration’s campaign to undermine our immigration laws,” it alleged that the EOIR does not have the authority to adopt the administrative-closure rule. Instead, it wrote, federal law requires an immigration judge, at the end of a proceeding, to “decide whether an alien is removable from the United States.”

Just a few hours after the case was filed, the DOJ and Texas asked O’Connor to enter a final judgment for the state. The DOJ also asked him both to throw out the rule altogether and to issue an order making clear that the EOIR could not adopt a similar rule in the future. O’Connor granted those requests on the same day.

On Aug. 7, three cities with large immigrant populations – Baltimore, Maryland; New Haven, Connecticut; and Columbus, Ohio – and Centro Legal de la Raza, which provides legal services to immigrants, filed an emergency motion to join the case so that they could defend the administrative-closure rule on appeal, when neither Texas nor the federal government intended to do so. O’Connor denied their request on the ground that they lacked a legal right to sue, known as standing. In particular, he rejected the cities’ contention that the elimination of the rule would cost them money because their taxpayers are likely to be deported.

The challengers then went to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 5th Circuit, which rejected their request to block the consent judgment between Texas and the Department of Justice and thereby reinstate the administrative-closure rule while their appeal continued.

On Oct. 9, the challengers came to the Supreme Court, calling the consent agreement the product of “egregious collusion” and asking the justices to step in. Their attorney, Joshua Salzman of Democracy Forward, argued that permitting the consent agreement to stand could have widespread implications. “If a judgment procured through such open collusion is allowed to remain in effect,” he wrote, “any agency can avoid the strictures of the” federal law governing administrative agencies “by advertising its unwillingness to defend a disfavored regulation and by immediately acquiescing to nationwide relief.”

Urging the Supreme Court to leave the agreement in place, U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer contended that the challengers’ request to pause O’Connor’s ruling “attempts to improperly leverage a clear-cut dispute over” the challengers’ efforts to join the case “into a far-reaching attack on the merits of” the court’s approval of the agreement. For its part, Texas told the justices that putting O’Connor’s ruling on hold “would revive a rule the district court declared unlawful, renew the fiscal and sovereign injuries Texas alleged, and unsettle a final judgment accepted by the actual parties.”

Four days after the case was fully briefed, the court denied the challengers’ request without comment.

Amy Howe is the co-founder of SCOTUSblog and its primary reporter.

#7783. A Roundtable Discussion on Genre Mashups and Shared Worlds

The following roundtable discussion features a variety of contributors to a new anthology, A Speculative Detective Agency: Case Files of the Supernatural and Fantastic, as they answer questions from editor Richie Narvaez. You can find copies of The Speculative Detective Agency here.

The new anthology A Speculative Detective Agency: Case Files of the Supernatural and Fantastic (Diversion Books, October 2026), edited by Matthew David Goodwin and Richie Narvaez, presents sixteen cross-genre stories set in a shared world in which an international group of investigators help people with their experiences of the unexplained. What appealed to you about writing within this shared reality?

Lincoln Michel: Fiction writing is typically a lonely enterprise where we lock ourselves in our rooms, chain ourselves to the keyboard, and howl into the void while we pound the keys. So writing in collaboration was a nice change of pace. The idea of a shared detective universe was a fun idea, and, for me at least, my best writing comes when I’m having fun.

Nadia Amina Rabbani: I really loved the idea of a shared world. For my story, “A Special Detective,” I took the information provided about the agency and themes I wanted to work with and wove them together. I did struggle with how to explicitly integrate the story with other stories. It felt almost sacrilegious to pilfer details from other stories even though I know that helps tie the world together.

Scott Adlerberg: I liked the idea of working within a set of ground rules all the contributors had to follow. That put constraints on the type of story we could all write, but at the same time, it left you free within those constraints to be as imaginative as possible. The challenge was to take those shared world points we had to use and to incorporate them into the story in as natural and unaffected a way as possible.

Victor De Anda: I found the shared reality of the SDA interesting, and constraints are always good. But it also felt wide open in terms of what else I could bring to the story. The real challenge for me was finding a way to bring something different to the mix. When I inquired to Richie about submissions, he told me that they already had plenty of ghost stories they were considering. So I brought in an old cryptid friend of mine, Ahuizotl.

Alex Grecian: I’m used to writing alone, but I’ve written a few comics and I like the idea (at least) of collaborating. This was collaboration, but without boundaries. I wrote the first draft, then read Monique Laban’s marvelous story “Anomaly Fixed” and things clicked into place. She wrote about possessed buildings and I was writing about the moon possessing people, so it was a no-brainer to incorporate her detective into my story.

“That juxtaposition between this wondrous, supernatural world and this dry, bureaucratic process was extremely funny to me…” –Monique Laban

Monique Laban: It’s counterintuitive, but what excited me most about contributing to this anthology was that it is premised on an organization’s renewal of its membership in a professional association based on the strength of its employees’ self-reported performance reviews. That juxtaposition between this wondrous, supernatural world and this dry, bureaucratic process was extremely funny to me and reminded me a lot of the 1997 movie Men in Black. With the idea that every agent had to share a recent job highlight, my main challenge was thinking of a mystery my agent could solve that would be notable without altering other agents’ potential missions. I considered, for instance, writing a story about the Winchester Mystery House, but worried a mission involving a location with that big of a reputation would require a more senior detective with more experience in, say, seances, and in “Anomaly Fixed,” I wanted to keep my junior agent’s skills more modest.

The anthology asks you mash up (at least) two genres. What is the value, do you think, in blending genres?

Nadia Amina Rabbani: One of the fun parts of working within a genre is playing with expectations. Readers approach a genre with the knowledge of the generally accepted boundaries and their own experience with it. When you mix genres, you get to pick and choose, splice and stitch pieces as serve the story and their own whims.

Monique Laban: I love mashups because they allow me to approach genres with new questions about why they work and what I enjoy about them; I always ask myself who I want to be in conversation with when I’m writing a new piece. This question inevitably becomes a fun excuse to make up what-if scenarios and build a syllabus for myself of materials I want to draw on. Such as, what if Nancy Drew grew a little jaded with her mysteries? What are normal employees at the Overlook Hotel like during its peak season? What if Shirley Jackson developed a video game? I really like to emphasize having fun and pulling from various sources, whether across genres, disciplines, and mediums, within my own process.

Victor De Anda: Mixing genres allows you to bring multiple elements into a story, which can be attractive to a reader, and gives a story more depth. The combination allows for a tension that pulls the reader in and makes the story a bit more memorable. At least that was my goal with “Hecho En Mexico.”

Scott Adlerberg: The value lies in building a story that can engage the reader in hopefully unexpected ways. You can create a strong sense of suspense, mystery, and unease, maybe even a touch of wonder. In particular, I love the zone where the mystery story meets the horror story. I like also where those two genres meet the psychological thriller. You can really evoke tension in that zone and a sense of ambiguity. Does a bizarre crime have a rational explanation, or will the solution involve the supernatural? If there’s a narrator, is that person reliable as a storyteller? By mashing up genres you can really take the reader, even in a short story, on an unpredictable journey.

Alex Grecian: I’ve always mashed up genres. Genre is a sales and marketing tool, and I don’t feel like it’s my responsibility to decide what category a story fits into. So as I’m writing, anything goes. There are hardcore readers of every genre, and I love them, but I think everyday readers want to come to something and be surprised.

Lincoln Michel: I know many writers, including some genre writers, scoff at the idea that genre means anything more than a marketing label. I disagree. I think genres are, in a sense, grand conversations that stretch through time. When you write in a genre, you are adding your voice to that conversation. You are agreeing with, rebutting, subverting, and building on the work that has come before. Mashing up genres lets you do that twice.

Genres come with certain reader expectations. For example, a whodunit reader wants a puzzle, or a horror reader wants to be unsettled. How did you try to satisfy those sets of expectations with your story?

Victor De Anda: I followed the story patterns from the X-Files TV show. A detective procedural that seems puzzling and Earthbound at first but is uncovered as something much more by the end. My goal was to offer both mystery and cryptid readers something different.

Alex Grecian: I keep those thoughts at bay when I’m writing. I never think in terms of genre. If I actually consider tropes or expectations, my tendency would be to try to subvert them, and that might not fit the story I’m writing. For “Tranquility” the only real question was whether the man was actually possessed by the moon, and I didn’t know that until I got to the climactic scene.

Nadia Amina Rabbani: As a reader, my mind can’t help but do wild conspiracy style boards with yarn connecting every dot. So, I try to write things that might surprise me if I were the reader, sometimes by subverting genre expectations.

Lincoln Michel: My favorite work tends to strike a balance between meeting and subverting expectations. If you meet the expectations too neatly, your work is formulaic. If you subvert incessantly, you likely lose what is appealing in the genre to begin with. I aim for a balance of meeting expectations enough to provide the pleasures of the genre—at least the pleasures as I see them—but still have enough surprise and strangeness that it feels unique to me.

Monique Laban: I chose a trope that I love shared between both genres: a glamorous setting, like Hercule Poirot on vacation or Eleanor Vance at Hill House. But beyond that, my instinct is to actually give myself even tighter restrictions and focus on sticking to arbitrary rules early on in drafting so that I can find the tone of the story first. So, my agent does not use dialogue tags even if other characters speak directly to her. This blending of her answers and her inner thoughts make for an eerie, not-quite-grounded environment that balances this feeling of hauntedness with the deliberate slow-burn of noir .

Scott Adlerberg: In “The Case of the Singular Hands,” I set up a situation where a man claims he is being haunted by something spectral and spooky. Then a killing occurs, and it happens in a locked room. So it’s basically a classic situation, using both horror and whodunit elements, and the story’s detective has to find out what’s behind the creepy phenomena and the murder. Is it something truly ghostly or something temporal?

Have you ever encountered something speculative yourself—a ghost, an alien, magic—and how did it affect you?

Lincoln Michel: All I can say is that I could give the SDA a lead or two to investigate . . .

Victor De Anda: Although I’ve never had an alien encounter, I’ve always wanted to. And I’ve always wondered whether the cattle mutilations we’ve heard about over the years were really performed by aliens, or by something much different.

Monique Laban: I have never had a speculative encounter. I think it’s partially because I want to experience one so badly. I once spent a weekend in the Hotel Monteleone and did everything I could to get possessed by the ghost of Tennessee Williams. Of course nothing happened, I wanted it too much.

Scott Adlerberg: I have not. And in all honesty, I’m not someone who is a believer in those things you’d classify as speculative. But I’m fascinated by the uncanny and the hard to explain regardless and in the psychology of people who do hew toward a belief in the speculative. That’s probably why I love reading that sort of fiction and why I love writing it.

Nadia Amina Rabbani: As a child, I was terrified of the dark. (This may or may not still be the case.) Every creak as the house settled, every movement in the corner of my eye was something monstrous out to get me. I was so scared I wouldn’t cry out to my parents for fear it would draw the darkness to me. I never vanquished whatever was stalking me and maybe it’s still there just outside my sight?

Richie Narvaez is the award-winning author of two novels and two short story collections. He teaches at Sarah Lawrence College and the Fashion Institute of Technology. His new anthology, The Speculative Detective Agency, is now available from Diversion Books.

#7782. Court Orders Plaintiff to File Handwritten Opposition,

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

after noting that many of plaintiff's filings contained seeming AI hallucinations, despite assertions in plaintiff's filings that all the citations were valid.

From Judge Aileen Cannon (S.D. Fla.) in Paulk v. Larva Labs, LLC, decided in June but just posted on Westlaw:

This case presents a dispute over Defendant's alleged fraudulent interference with Plaintiff's Non-Fungible Tokens ("NFTs"). Plaintiff's Complaint, initially filed in Florida state court on January 20, 2026, alleges that in June 2017, Plaintiff used a publicly available software tool to generate 141 NFTs on the Ethereum blockchain. Each of these NFTs represents ownership of a unique CryptoPunk that was part of the first version of CryptoPunks ("V1"), a pioneering generative art project consisting of 24x24 pixel portraits. To create the NFTs, Plaintiff paid only nominal "gas fees" (i.e., fees paid to third parties who validate transactions on the Ethereum blockchain), and the NFTs "have remained in [a] dormant wallet" controlled to this day by Plaintiff.

Plaintiff alleges that, on June 23, 2017, Defendant "deployed" a second version of CryptoPunks ("V2"), "claiming V1 contained a 'bug.'" The Complaint then asserts that Defendant "suppressed V1 marketplace activity while promoting V2 as the sole authoritative collection, rendering Plaintiff's assets commercially impaired". Based on these allegations, the Complaint asserts causes of action for fraudulent concealment (Count I), unjust enrichment (Count II), declaratory relief (Count III), and injunctive relief (Count IV), seeking unspecified monetary damages and an injunction.

The court discussed various procedural issues, and then added:

As a separate matter, the Court is concerned more generally about the plethora of legal filings seemingly prepared by artificial intelligence and submitted by Plaintiff that make frivolous and unsupported arguments to the Court [see, e.g., ECF Nos. 15, 16, 17, 18, 19, 26, 26-1, 31, 32, 33]. As an example, Plaintiff makes the obviously incorrect submission that the citizenship of Defendant's counsel can be considered in determining complete diversity.

And many of Plaintiff's filings contain disclaimers to the Court, expressly certifying "that every legal authority, statutory provision, rule of procedure, and historical case citation referenced within [the filings] has been independently read, analyzed, verified, and cross-referenced against official federal and state legal repositories." In each of these filings, "Plaintiff guarantees that every cited case stands as valid, binding law within the United States Supreme Court and the Eleventh Circuit Court of Appeals, possesses an active and unchecked standing, and accurately represents the procedural postures asserted." And he expressly warrants that he has not included any "fictitious or unverified citations," and that he has "manually double-checked" each case to ensure that it "support[s] Plaintiff's cause perfectly, ensuring that no unverified or 'hallucinated' data is presented to the Court."

No doubt Plaintiff's artificial intelligence legal counsel told him to say all this. And the AI certainly had the right idea—litigants should not make misrepresentations to the Court. Unfortunately, Plaintiff did not practice what his artificial counsel preached. Instead, he cites to "Snapper v. Redan, 523 U.S. 83 (1998)"—a case which does not exist—for the proposition that "when a company's chief legal representative has been sent formal notification at a publicly advertised professional office location, the entity cannot assert an administrative breakdown within its secondary commercial mail hubs as an equitable basis to vacate an otherwise valid default". Notwithstanding the made-up citation, the case Plaintiff means to cite, Snapper, Inc. v. Redan (11th Cir. 1999), is an Eleventh Circuit case that says nothing of the sort. Instead, Snapper established that federal appellate courts have jurisdiction to review remand orders based on the enforcement of contractual forum selection clauses. It does not mention vacatur, or default, or even mail—and it certainly does not stand for the extremely narrow proposition for which Plaintiff cites it.

In light of all this, Plaintiff has violated his duty of candor to the Court and has committed a Rule 11 violation…. [T]he Court [therefore] imposes filing sanctions as follows:

Plaintiff failed to respond to the motion to dismiss, and in a later opinion the court granted that motion.

#7779. Lawyer, business partner accused of defrauding cannabis investor of $750K

A Los Angeles attorney and his business partner are accused of paying for their personal expenses with investor money instead of funding business-to-consumer cannabis trade shows. (Image from Shutterstock)

A Los Angeles attorney and his business partner are accused of paying for their personal expenses with investor money instead of funding business-to-consumer cannabis trade shows, including the unsuccessful Green Street Festival in 2022.

A Los Angeles County court complaint filed by investor Jamie Chisick alleged that attorney Joshua Shelton of the Winston Wolfe Law Firm and his business partner, Rama Mayo, took $750,000 for a 15% ownership stake in the Green Street Symposium.

According to the Oct. 19 complaint, Shelton and Mayo, cannabis entrepreneurs, promised to organize large trade events that would attract thousands of attendees and generate “millions of dollars in revenue,” according to coverage on Law360.

Chisick obtained documents that he said shows that his money had been used for “personal payments, including but not limited to private jets, health insurance, bar dues (Shelton) and general overhead unrelated to GSS operations.”

The 2022 Green Street Festival brought in about $190,000 with about $178,000 refunded. A 2023 festival with projections of attracting over 10,000 attendees and up to $4.7 million in revenue drew a smaller crowd and did not produce a profit.

Chisick seeks to recover his investment and punitive damages, according to the complaint.

#7778. Three Italian Heist Films You Need to See

Ciao ragazzi! Benvenuti! I love Italian cinema, especially from the 1950s and 60s. I’ve been treating myself to the lighthearted crime films of Dino Risi (more on that soon), lately, but I’ve been meaning to rewatch a delightful trifecta of Italian crime comedies starring the beloved star Vittorio Gassman, Italy’s “Il Mattatore” (so-called after a Risi film that he leads). Now that Halloween is over, and we can return to our normal crime programing, I thought we should kick things off Italian-style. Check these out. The first one is genuinely one of the best capers ever made, and the sequels are a lot of fun.

Mario Monicelli directs a crack cast in this wonderful Italian caper which stole my heart. Spoofing Rififi a little bit, it’s a perfect gem of a comedy—Vittorio Gassman plays Giuseppe “Peppe il Pantera” Baiocchi, a petty crook with dreams of being a big-time thief, who plans a perfect pawnshop heist on a quiet block in Rome. But once word gets out about his plot, all manner of unscrupulous characters come out of the woodwork and hope to take part in it. It’s an ensemble cast like you’ve never seen before (hello Marcello!), a phenomenal farce, and an all around fantastico time.

This sequel to Big Deal on Madonna Street sets our favorite band of thieves (still led by Il Mattatore!) after a big-time heist. This time, they have to steal a suitcase of money (containing the pool of bets over soccer tournaments). As you might expect with these guys, though, things don’t go according to plan. Unfortunately, the sequel is not as good as the first, but hey, Claudia Cardinale is in this one!

This sequel to Fiasco in Milan doesn’t live up to the second and definitely doesn’t live up the first, although it does at least attempt to do something new, rather than repeat the success of the first film. In this third chapter, directed by Amanzio Todini, Tiberio (Marcello Mastroianni) is now the main character, fresh out of prison and reuiniting with his old friends from the gang, Peppe (our hero from the last two movies) and Ferribotte.

#7777. Anna Rasche on the Hope diamond and the trope of cursed jewels in literature

Each year approximately six million people visit the Hall of Minerals in the Smithsonian Museum of Natural History to jostle for a glimpse of the infamous Hope Diamond. Many are afraid to get too close. This singular stone has passed through the hands of adventurers and royalty, heiresses and actresses. And according to legend it brought almost all of them to a bad end.

Today, the Hope epitomizes the “cursed gem.” An object as alluring as it is dangerous; all the wealth of a kingdom, condensed into something that could be forgotten in a coat pocket. But it is hardly alone. Evil jewelry lurks in our earliest mythologies, embeds itself in the pages of history books, and stands at the center of some of our most celebrated works of modern literature.

An early example is the cursed Necklace of Harmonia, wrought by a cuckolded Hephaestus, Greek god of the forge, as a passive-aggressive wedding gift for the daughter born of his wife’s infidelity. Nonnus describes the necklace as a golden tangle of snakes and eagles, encrusted with gems. The tragedies of Oedipus and that of Acteon, who was torn apart by his own hunting dogs, can be traced to this sinister family heirloom.

In India, the Sanskrit texts of the Bhagavata Purana tell of the Syamantaka, a jewel, perhaps a ruby, gifted by the god Surya to the mortal King Satrajit.

The Purana states: “It was the peculiar virtue of that gem, that if worn with all purity it would yield gold and prosperity of the kingdom but if worn by a man of bad character it would bring on his death.”

Indeed, as soon as the stone was in mortal hands it set off a chain of violent deaths. The impure men who possessed it were mauled by a lion, murdered in their sleep, and decapitated. Historians Anita Anand and William Dalrymple hypothesize that the legend of the Syamantaka is the original “curse” legend, one so often attached to important Indian gems.

In the seventeenth century the French gem merchant Jean-Baptiste Tavernier traveled to India, unbothered by any tales of curses. He returned to the court of Louis XIV with spectacular diamonds from the fabled mines of Golconda. One of them would eventually be recut into the Hope diamond. Though Tavernier wrote hundreds of pages about his travels, he never told how he acquired the blue diamond (good business for a gem merchant).

In the absence of a true account, a rumor took hold. It was said that Tavernier prised it from the eye of an idol, invoking a terrible curse. Word spread that he, like Acteon, was eaten by dogs.

What is known for certain is that this blue diamond was stolen during the French Revolution, smuggled into England, and recut to hide its royal French provenance. It reappeared decades later and significantly lighter, in the collection of banker Henry Phillip Hope. Today, most gemologists agree that the missing carats became dust on the cutter’s wheel.

But for a long time it was believed another stone was cut, a blue brilliant of about ten carats. It was said to be owned by the mad Duke of Brunswick, a voracious collector of gems who died exiled from his ancestral seat. The duke’s effects were sold at auction and the blue diamond disappeared. The Brunswick Blue is the mysterious stone, a maybe-sister of the Hope, that inspired the fictional gem called the Midnight in my novel, The Cursed Diamond.

The Hope reemerged in England in the1830s, amid a Gothic Revival where cursed jewels fit right into the zeitgeist. Anne of Geierstein by Sir Walter Scott, published 1829, tells of Lady Hermione, who turned to ash when her precious opal was touched by holy water. (It was Scott’s fiction that launched the still-enduring superstition of opals as unlucky stones). Murky origins aside, the Hope was displayed as a national treasure at London’s Great Exposition of 1851, alongside another Indian diamond with a sinister history.

The Koh-I-Noor, the “mountain of light,” was once a principal treasure of the Mughal Empire. It came into British possession in 1849 after a particularly heartless agent of the British East India Company extorted it from the last Maharaja of the Sikh Empire, the ten-year-old Duleep Singh. The ship that carried the stone to England was plagued by tempests and cholera.

When it was finally presented to Queen Victoria, she accepted it with reluctance, believing it cursed. Luckily for her, an addendum was soon added: the curse only applied to men. To this day the Koh-I-Noor remains in the Crown Jewels of the United Kingdom, a source of contention with India.

Inspired by the Koh-I-Noor, Wilkie Collins invented The Moonstone—the fictional yellow diamond at the center of his 1868 bestselling novel. In this ur-detective novel, a young Englishwoman lands in trouble after inheriting a gem stolen from a Hindu idol by her unsavory soldier uncle. The Moonstone’s success fixed the typical arc of a cursed jewel in the western imagination: illicit origins, greed-induced folly, and bitter ends for those who coveted what was never theirs.

In 1901 Lord Francis Hope sold his family’s blue diamond to cover debts he’d racked up partying his way around the globe with then-wife, American actress May Yohé (Yohé would die in impoverished obscurity, blaming the Hope Diamond for her troubles). For the next eight years the gem passed quietly between dealers and buyers, landing with famed jeweler Pierre Cartier.

Soon, newspapers were cataloguing the misfortunes of the Hope’s previous owners: kingdoms lost, carriages overturned, ships wrecked, heads removed. It is a dark and un-fact-checked history, allegedly encouraged by Cartier to add intrigue and close a sale with American gold heiress Evalyn Walsh McClean and her husband.

After the McCleans purchased the diamond, their lives were marred by tragedy: madness, addiction, political scandal, and accidental deaths. Even so, Evalyn wore the Hope until her death. “Bad luck objects, for me, are lucky,” she said.

The trope of the cursed jewel, a treasure that brings great joy and great sorrow, continues to captivate and inspire works of fiction. It lives in Tolkien’s One Ring. It goes on and on as the Heart of the Ocean in Titanic and burns bright as the Sea of Flames in All the Light We Cannot See. Now, in The Cursed Diamond, it manifests as an icy blue stone called the Midnight, my own humble addition to this enduring lore.

Anna Rasche is a historian and gemologist who has previously worked in the jewelry collection at the Metropolitan Museum of Art and as a curatorial fellow at the Cooper Hewitt, Smithsonian Design Museum. Rasche's debut is based on original research she conducted on the uses of gemstones in medieval medicine at the Cooper Hewitt Museum and on site in Italy. She lives in Brooklyn with her husband and infant daughter.
