#7730. Five November criminal law arguments, and one last look at the 2025-26 term

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

While all eyes are on what seem like inevitable Supreme Court election law “emergency” petitions, it may be comforting to realize that the regular business of the Supreme Court still goes on. Argument calendars released months ago show five criminal law and related cases set for argument in November. Below are some quick summaries of them. But first, an announcement and one more quick look at last term.

My ABA “Annual Review of the Supreme Court’s Term: Criminal Cases”

For some 30 years I have written and the American Bar Association has published an “Annual Review of the Supreme Court’s Term: Criminal Cases” for the prior term. This is a booklet of manageable size for persons interested in a complete picture of the hundreds of pages the justices write every year on topics and cases related to criminal law. That’s also what this regular SCOTUSblog column aims to do – but the review provides a lot more detail. This effort – and believe me, it takes hours to compile – is a fun and (I hope) useful part of my pro bono work.

This year’s booklet will be published here on the ABA Criminal Justice Section‘s website next week. It is downloadable, and while I hold the copyright, anyone can use and distribute it. Summaries of 45 merits decisions and 26 separate writings by justices on the orders docket last term are included, as well as 14 criminal law and related cases granted for argument (so far) this term can be found in it as well. If you enjoy the booklet or have suggestions or criticisms, please let me know.

Before getting to the November sitting, here’s one interesting question from last term (more can be found in the booklet) that only recently occurred to me regarding two pairs of very different cases: Olivier v. City of Brandon versus Fernandez v. United States, and Hunter v. United States versus Clark v. Sweeney. At a high level of generality, is one case in each pair inconsistent with the other?

In brief, the court ruled in Fernandez that doubts about a prior conviction must be pursued in habeas, not the federal compassionate relief statute. Two months earlier in Olivier, however, the court ruled that a prospective challenge to a statute under which a person was previously convicted need not be pursued under habeas but instead can be filed under §1983 – even though that challenge might well “imply the invalidity of Olivier’s conviction.” Justice Elena Kagan wrote Olivier for a unanimous court, while Justice Amy Coney Barrett wrote Fernandez in an 8 to 1 result.

Similarly, in Clark v. Sweeney the court summarily reversed the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 4th Circuit for granting habeas relief on grounds not argued by the parties. But then, seven months later in the term in Hunter, the court ruled that a court of appeals can ignore a waiver of appeal if a “miscarriage of justice” is perceived – presumably even if that miscarriage has not been raised by the parties. The court emphasized that the independence, discretion, and “integrity” of the judiciary is at stake. Again, the votes were not close: Hunter (Kagan again) was 8-1, and Clark was an apparently unanimous summary reversal.

I wrote separately about both Clark and Hunter in columns last term, and now, the broad overview of all the decisions together occasioned by compiling my booklet led me to comparisons not apparent at the time. The pairings I have identified are not directly inconsistent, and cases can always be distinguished from each other on a granular level. But at some general level I think there are clear tensions between the animating philosophies in each pair. Those tensions reflect deep differences among the justices on fundamental liberty and fairness questions reflected in their approach to criminal law. More of which we turn to now.

As indicated in my September column about upcoming criminal cases, December will be a “big” month, with AR-15 rifle possession and “forfeiture for a six-pack of beer” set for argument on Dec. 1 and 2. One criminal case, Beaird v. United States, has already been argued, presenting a relatively abstract question about how much deference to give to federal Sentencing Guidelines commentary notes. But November will be action-packed with five cases related to criminal law.

To be fair, none of the five cases raises what I would call a “pure” criminal law issue. Instead, there’s a variety of topics related to criminal law: habeas corpus rules (two cases), immigration, private causes of action for constitutional violations, and a purely civil procedure case arising from the firing of a supervisory assistant district attorney. But all present interesting legal issues for Supreme Court nerds like me (us?). Here are brief thumbnail sketches, in order of my own level of interest, not their respective argument dates.

For pure fireworks among the justices, the oral argument a week from Monday may be quite a show. But the result seems pretty much preordained: the court will either overrule an old civil rights precedent or once again limit it to its exact facts.

In 1970, the liberal Warren court ruled in Bivens v. Six Unknown Federal Narcotics Agents that individuals may sue federal officials directly under the constitution for damages caused if they have violated the Constitution, despite there being no statute that provides for such a “cause of action.” The vote was 5+1 to 3 and the decision has been controversial ever since. Multiple justices have said or suggested that without a congressional statute approving such claims, Bivens violates the constitutional separation of powers. Over time, and with changing personnel and views on the court, Bivens has thus repeatedly been limited, with the court declining to extend it to other circumstances over a dozen times.

In the instant case, Kekai Watanabe was attacked in a federal prison gang riot, and he alleges that he was denied medical care (with prison paramedic Francis Nielsen allegedly saying “stop being a cry baby”) and instead placed in solitary confinement for months. Only then was a serious spinal column injury identified and addressed. In 1980, the Supreme Court had extended Bivens (which had been based on the Fourth Amendment) to Eighth Amendment deliberate indifference claims. But that was the last time the court has ever looked favorably on Bivens. Nielsen now asks that Bivens be overruled, while the solicitor general suggests more mildly that the court might wait for a Fourth Amendment case to do the same.

At oral argument, I have no doubt that the three liberal justices will speak vigorously for Bivens and about the injustice of not allowing remedies for wrongs that violate the Bill of Rights. Chief Justice John Marshall’s famous invocation of the maxim “every right ... must have a remedy,” in Marbury v, Madison, will almost certainly be brought up. But just as vigorously, other justices will invoke the constitutional separation of powers and say that it is Congress, and not an unelected judiciary, that must write legislative protections for legal wrongs. The rhetorical and emotional heroics in this argument may rival those heard in voting, abortion, and birthright citizenship cases. Yet an anti-Bivens result seems virtually pre-ordained.

When a federal prisoner is nearing the end of their term of imprisonment, they often can be transferred to a “halfway house,” which is just what it sounds like: the prisoner is confined to a group home setting at night, but free to leave during the day (with conditions) to look for employment, attend rehabilitation programs, and the like. The prisoner is still within the government’s control and supervision. But is a halfway house “custody” so that legal aspects of it – or in this case, alleged entitlement to it – can be challenged in a habeas corpus proceeding?

Richard Cooke has published on SCOTUSblog a nice account of the issues and briefed arguments. William Maxwell, a mafia-affiliated fraudster who was sentenced in 2015 to 20 years in federal prison, filed a habeas petition claiming that he is entitled to “accelerated release” to a halfway house. The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 5th Circuit affirmed dismissal, ruling that habeas does not encompass a mere transfer between prison settings. As Cooke writes, the issue is “tricky” because prior cases have used various words to describe the reach of the federal habeas statute, including one (back in 1973) that habeas corpus can extend to a claim for “good conduct” time credits. The federal habeas statute explicitly also addresses prisoners “in custody,” but then lists specifics that don’t quite capture the claim here. And yet, a halfway house is certainly a “level of custody,” even if less restrictive than prison. Moreover, if Maxwell can’t use habeas, he does not appear to have any other judicial remedy available, because 42 U.S.C. §1983 (which authorizes people to sue state officials for violating a constitutional right) can’t be applied to federal officials (as noted in my description of Watanabe).

Neither the solicitor general nor Maxwell liked the 5th Circuit’s description of the proper habeas analysis. So a former law clerk of Justice Samuel Alito has been appointed to argue for affirmance here. Folks who love the intricacies of habeas law – imagine tax law mavens but in criminal law – will find the Maxwell arguments fascinating. But I imagine that the overall numbers of listeners who tune in for Monday’s live argument – has anyone ever filed a FOIA request to get those numbers? – won’t be very high.

This is another case involving the intricacies of habeas law. And it is founded on a complicated procedural history, which is often the case in state criminal cases that finally make their way to the Supreme Court after multiple rounds of lower court litigation. Statutes that regulate habeas petitions filed by both federal and state prisoners permit successive habeas petitions to go forward, even if a prior habeas petition has been filed and denied, if the new petition raises a “new rule of constitutional law ... that was previously unavailable.” The question presented here seems relatively simple (after the procedural thicket is penetrated): is a rule “previously unavailable” when it was “practically unavailable” because the federal courts with jurisdiction over the prisoner would have automatically denied it?

Dexter Johnson is on death row in Texas and says he is intellectually disabled. In 2002, the Supreme Court ruled in Atkins v. Virginia that intellectually disabled persons are protected from execution under the Eighth Amendment’s cruel and unusual punishment ban. In 2015, the 5th Circuit denied a habeas petition Johnson had filed, but then in 2017 the Supreme Court issued a decision that Texas’ definition of intellectual disability was wrong. That is, a new psychiatric Diagnostic Manual allowed a person like Johnson to be declared intellectually disabled. Johnson then filed a successive habeas petition arguing that the change in Texas law created a “new rule” allowing an Atkins claim in his jurisdiction, which had been “previously unavailable” because circuit precedent had declared it meritless. In other words, Johnson says the 2002 Atkins rule was “unavailable” to him until 2017, because it would have been a waste of time, even frivolous, for him to file it prior to the change in the legal standard for Atkins protection. The 5th Circuit appears to have accepted that idea in the litigation leading to this case.

At oral argument next Wednesday, plain language textualists may have a field day. The Atkins ruling was clearly available prior to 2017, and Texas argues, quite simply, that its new constitutional rule was thus not “unavailable” when Johnson filed his first habeas petition. However, as Johnson contends, “available” is variously defined as “capable of being employed with advantage” or “usable.” He therefore argues that the Atkins rule was simply not usable – it was “previously unavailable” to him – until the legal standard for Atkins was made clear in 2017.

It thus turns out that the statutory phrase at issue here is not “plain,” but rather subject to different textual interpretations. Which means, I think, that the oral argument is likely to fall back (as is often the case in habeas cases) on the ideological orientations of various justices. It will be the kind of semantic battling and linguistic nitpicking that, although obviously important, can make the average American simply sick of lawyers.

Although this important immigration case will be argued on the first day of what insiders call “the December calendar,” it actually occurs on the last day of November, when some of us may still be eating Thanksgiving leftovers. Like Guerrero, the case involves the practical application of a simple phrase that literally might mean something else.

There are two noncitizen cases consolidated in one petition here, but discussing the lead respondent is enough for today. Tamer Wassily is a noncitizen who was granted asylum in the United States in 2000, and the applicable statute says that “any alien granted asylum” is eligible for adjustment to permanent resident status. The twist is that Wassily’s asylum status was terminated in 2004 following his conviction of a crime. The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 2nd Circuit ruled that “granted asylum” must mean “presently be granted asylum” and so it does not encompass applicants whose asylum status is later terminated. The solicitor general agrees, contending that a “common-sense understanding” of the statute must mean that a person who was once granted asylum status which was later terminated cannot take advantage of that prior status. In opposition, Wassily takes the textual position that the unqualified statutory phrase “any alien granted asylum” describes him, and the statute says nothing about a later revocation.

One might cynically guess how this case will come out, but that is not what interests me most. Instead, note how the textualist arguments flip between Guerrero and Wassily. The government seeks a simple plain meaning result for “previously unavailable” in Guerrero but wants a non-textual “common-sense” interpretation in Wassily. There’s nothing wrong with using different arguments in different cases – that’s what law and lawyers are for (smiling emoji). But I sure wish these two cases were being argued on the same day: the combined debate between textualist and commonsense-driven justices and their ideologies likely switching in mere hours might make our heads spin.

Younge v. Fulton Judicial Circuit District Attorney’s Office, Georgia (Nov. 2)

Finally, if you feel like Maxwell (described above) might be a bit of a snoozer, wait until the next argument the same day. I wouldn't include Jasmine Younge here at all if she weren't a fired supervisory prosecutor suing her former district attorney office. According to Younge, she was fired about two weeks after telling her boss that she was pregnant. She sued on the basis of pregnancy discrimination, and only months later did the DA’s office invoke a statutory exemption to pregnancy discrimination statutes, something the office had not asserted in its answer to Younge’s complaint or earlier discovery maneuvers. The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 11th Circuit affirmed judgment for the DA’s office on that exception, saying there had been no prejudice to Younge from the DA’s delay in bringing up this affirmative defense. Other circuits have ruled that an affirmative defense simply cannot be raised that late – so we are off to the races.

Rodger Citron writes for this blog that the case “will quicken the pulse of civil procedure afficionados.” I’ll be calmer, listening with only one ear to hear how the DA’s attorney explains how they missed the statutory exemption, as well as wondering whether the number of listeners has gone up or down from the Maxwell argument immediately prior.

Rory Little has been teaching Constitutional and Criminal Law topics at UC Law SF (formerly Hastings) for over 30 years, after 12 years of practice.

Recommended Citation: Rory Little, Five November criminal law arguments, and one last look at the 2025-26 term, SCOTUSblog (Oct. 30, 2026, 9:30 AM), https://www.scotusblog.com/2026/10/five-november-criminal-law-arguments-and-one-last-look-at-the-2025-26-term/

#7729. Pactiv Evergreen settles for $6.25M over 2023 North Carolina mill closure

The restitution amount is more than half of what Pactiv Evergreen received from the state in economic development grants for the site.

The paper mill in Canton had been in operation for more than 100 years prior to then-owner Pactiv shutting it down in 2023, according to the state of North Carolina. Blue Ridge Paper Products operated the facility since 1999, and in 2007 that company became Evergreen Packaging through a merger. Pactiv Evergreen formed in 2020 through the combination of Evergreen Packaging and Pactiv, both of which were previously acquired by Reynolds Group Holdings.

At the time of the Canton mill’s closure, many people expressed surprise at Pactiv Evergreen’s decision. The company made the announcement in March 2023 along with other closure and restructuring disclosures, and CEO Mike King noted a “challenging market environment” for Pactiv’s beverage merchandising business. North Carolina Gov. Roy Cooper said in a statement last week that the Canton closure came as a “gut punch" to the local and state economies.

Upon introducing the lawsuit in May 2024, then-Attorney General Josh Stein noted that taxpayers “invested in Pactiv Evergreen to bolster our state’s economy,” but Pactiv didn’t hold up its end of the bargain. He said at the time that his office had tried working with Pactiv for a year to address the company’s obligations, but it had “become clear that legal action was necessary to hold Pactiv accountable.” The initial lawsuit sought repayment of the full $12 million in economic incentives that Pactiv had received.

The settlement should not be viewed as an admission to wrongdoing, according to the North Carolina Department of Justice.

“Pactiv broke its promise to the state and the people of Canton, and today’s settlement holds it accountable for violating its agreement,” Attorney General Jeff Jackson, who was elected in November and took office last month, said of the new settlement. “This settlement will allow the people of Canton and Haywood County to immediately put millions back into rebuilding their economy after the mill’s closure, and it will shield them from future litigation from Pactiv.”

The candidates for state attorney general repeatedly brought up the mill issues on the campaign trail prior to November’s election. Both candidates expressed a desire to hold Pactiv accountable.

Pactiv had filed a motion to dismiss the complaint in July 2024. But a judge denied that motion in October, allowing the lawsuit to proceed.

“We are pleased to have resolved with the State of North Carolina all outstanding matters relating to the closure and sale of our former Canton mill site. We thank our employees for their contributions to our company and wish the Canton community well in this next chapter for the Town,” said Pactiv Evergreen Tuesday in an emailed statement.

This wasn’t Pactiv’s first legal battle over the Canton site.

In autumn 2023, the company reached a settlement worth more than $2 million with the U.S. EPA over Clean Air Act violations at Canton. Earlier that year, the North Carolina Department of Environmental Quality said the site violated water quality requirements; the company denied the allegations. In 2021 and 2022, the mill faced state air quality violations.

Novolex is in the process of acquiring Pactiv Evergreen for $6.7 billion. The deal, which would take Pactiv private, is expected to close during the first half of this year.

#7727. EU legal adviser finds limited uses of Google AI could run afoul of publishers’ rights

A court adviser urged judges to leave AI training questions aside and examine how Gemini fetches and repackages journalism.

(CN) â Googleâs chatbot can poach a newspaperâs readers without breaking copyright law, but serving up a recognizable substitute for its stories is another matter, an adviser to Europeâs top court said Tuesday.

Hungarian publisher Like Company is asking a Budapest court to find that Google Ireland infringed its rights by using its articles without permission through Bard, now called Gemini. The Hungarian court sought guidance from the Court of Justice of the European Union, in the court’s first case over generative AI.

In a nonbinding opinion, Advocate General Maciej SzpunarÂ advisedÂ setting aside AI training questions as hypothetical: Nothing supported the claim that Likeâs articles trained Gemini, and training fell outside the specific publishersâ right invoked.

He concentrated on the chatbot retrieving articles to answer usersâ questions.

That process could infringe publishersâ rights through unlawful access, including bypassing effective paywalls or bot barriers, or through answers that recognizably reproduced an articleâs expression enough to replace the original entirely. Rewording is not necessarily enough to avoid infringement. Making a publication available to the public would additionally require such reuse to appear systematically in answers to related questions.

The protection covered an articleâs arrangement, structure and phrasing. Invoking freedom to share and receive information, Szpunar wrote: âUnder that freedom, in a democratic society, no one should be granted an exclusive right over information as such.â

Providers could be responsible where infringement was inherent in their business model or they failed to take appropriate preventive measures. Likeâs example appeared not to meet his conditions, Szpunar said, leaving the factual assessment to the Hungarian court.

An unlikely subject supplied the test: dolphins. In July 2023, Like reported on Hungarian singer KozsÃ³âs longstanding ambition to create an aquarium at Lake Balaton. Asked to summarize the coverage, Googleâs chatbot drew on the article. Like depended on advertising revenue from website visits; an answer on Google could give readers one less reason to click through.

At the March hearing, Likeâs lawyer described the example as part of a broader pattern of unpaid reuse that threatened publishersâ bargaining power. Googleâs lawyers countered that Gemini predicted words rather than retrieved stored articles, so similarities did not establish copying. They said no specific reproduction had been proved.

A 2019 European lawÂ gave publishers control over certain online reuse of their publications to help them recover their investment. Like invoked that narrower protection, rather than copyright generally.

Nicola Lucchi, a professor of comparative law at Barcelonaâs Pompeu Fabra University, warned that rewritten summaries could drain publishersâ traffic and advertising revenue while escaping that protection.

âThe small Hungarian publisher in this case seems unlikely to obtain much relief,â he said.

Lucchi challenged Szpunarâs rejection of an argument he developed with fellow scholar Tim Dornis that AI-generated content competing with works used to train it could undermine their normal commercial exploitation. Szpunar treated that displacement as ordinary competition, a distinction Lucchi disputed.

He questioned training opt-outs that could cost publishers search visibility and the opinionâs inconsistent comparisons with human learning and memory. He welcomed easier proof of article use but favored direct obligations on platforms over proving each infringement, and highlighted possible national compensation schemes.

Szpunar nevertheless examined training extensively. Copies made for training could generally qualify for Europeâs exception for automated text analysis, provided access was lawful and rights holders had not validly opted out. Fetching articles for specific answers served a different purpose, and those technical copies might instead qualify for an exception for temporary copying, depending on access and the resulting answer.

Google welcomed the training analysis, calling the text-analysis exemptions vital to European competitiveness and AI development.

âGemini learns linguistic patterns to create original outputs rather than replicating content, supported by extensive publisher controls that give rightsholders clear choice and the ability to opt out,â a spokesperson said.

Angela Mills Wade, executive director of the European Publishers Council, welcomed the rejection of automatic consent from freely accessible journalism. She emphasized enforcing access restrictions and website rights reservations without losing search visibility. But she questioned using an exception dating to 2001 to justify competing AI answers without a license, backing negotiated deals that preserved publishersâ bargaining power.

âEuropeâs commitment to journalism must be reflected in rights that work in practice,â she said.

JoÃ£o Pedro Quintais, an associate professor of information law at the University of Amsterdam, highlighted the demanding threshold for replacing an article and the safeguards expected of providers. On overseas training, he said: âThe AG is skeptical that downstream EU market effects alone are sufficient, and suggests that the legislature should provide a clearer solution.â

PÃ©ter Mezei, a professor of law at the University of Szeged, cautioned against treating the opinion as an answer to every AI copyright question, given the narrower protection afforded to press publishers. He highlighted Szpunarâs skepticism that reproduced text proved a model stored copies of protected works, and stressed that a training exception did not authorize later uses. Pointing to two further pending Gemini referrals, he said: âThese are only the first steps toward clarifying the concerns at hand.â

Like Company did not respond to a request for comment.

The opinion is advice, not an appealable judgment. The EU judges must now issue their ruling, which the Budapest court will apply to resolve the dispute.

Courthouse News reporter Eunseo Hong is based in the Netherlands.

#7725. Judge who invoked role in garbage fine battle admonished

A judicial misconduct watchdog said a Brooklyn, New York City, judge repeatedly invoked her judicial role and trial schedule while contesting New York City sanitation citations for garbage in front of her home. (Photo from Shutterstock)

A judicial misconduct watchdog said a Brooklyn, New York City, judge repeatedly invoked her judicial role and trial schedule while contesting New York City sanitation citations for garbage in front of her home.

The New York State Commission on Judicial Conduct admonished Judge Katherine A. Levine of the Kings County Supreme Court in New York, noting that she had served as a judge since 2008 without prior disciplinary issues. The commission determination, dated Oct. 2, was announced Monday.

The conduct took place between March 2024 through November 2025 and was connected to three citations. During this time, Levine repeatedly mentioned her judicial status and responsibilities when communicating about hearings and fines, according to the commission determination.

“Invoking judicial office to avoid paying a fine undermines public confidence in the integrity of the judiciary and suggests that judges are exempt from rules that apply to everyone else,” said commission administrator Robert H. Tembeckjian, according to a story by Law360. “The Office of Administrative Trials and Hearings was right not to give special treatment to a judge.”

#7724. DC Circuit signals ICE ban on surprise lawmaker oversight visits unlawful

U.S. Circuit Judge Robert Wilkins said the policy could hypothetically be compared to government officials barring lawmakers from the Senate chambers, as oversight and voting are part of lawmakers' official duties.

WASHINGTON (CN) â A D.C. Circuit panel appeared likely Tuesday to side with a group of Democratic House members in their lawsuit challenging a Department of Homeland Security policy blocking surprise oversight visits at immigration detention centers.

The three-judge panel made up of U.S. Circuit Judges Robert Wilkins, Gregory Katsas and Bradley Garcia â a Barack Obama, Donald Trump and Joe Biden appointee, respectively â heard the Justice Departmentâs challenge to a federal judgeâs Feb. 2 order freezing the requirement that lawmakers provide a weekâs notice to conduct a visit.

A group of 13 Democratic lawmakers, led by Colorado Representative Joe Neguse, filed the lawsuit in July 2025 and argued a recurring provision in each congressional appropriations bill since 2020 specifically bars the department from using its appropriated funds to prevent lawmakers from conducting oversight visits.

The specific provision in the latest congressional appropriation bill in 2024, Section 527, also prohibits DHS from using the funds to make any temporary modification that in âany way alters what is observed by a visiting Member of Congress.â

According to the Justice Department, the funds appropriated in 2024 to U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement expired in February 2026, thus rendering U.S. District Judge Jia Cobbâs order to comply with Section 527 effectively moot.

Justice Department attorney Steven Myers urged the panel to restore the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement policy, arguing the lawmakers lack standing to claim an injury to their official powers, and the policy impacts all members equally.

He pointed to the 1997 Supreme Court case Raines v. Byrd, which he argued set the precedent that lawmakers lack standing to assert injuries to their powers that arise âsolely because they are members of Congress.â

âOn the one hand, legislators might have standing to assert that theyâve been deprived of something to which they are personally entitled, what Raines describes as the loss of a private right,â Myers said. âThose are things like the loss of salary or a loss of your own personal seat in the legislature. But in contrast, Raines says a claimed injury to official authority or power that arises solely because they are members of Congress does not state an Article III controversy.â

Wilkins, at the tail end of the hearing, directly challenged the governmentâs position with a series of hypotheticals in which the Department of Homeland Security closes streets surrounding the U.S. Capitol, blocks entrances to the Capitol and surrounding office buildings, or even the Senate chamber doors, all to pass a Trump-sponsored bill.

Myers said any example would be a hard case for the government to win, but the question would center on whether âentering your place of workâ amounts to an injury to an official power.

âYou donât know that thereâs a clear yes or no answer to that?â Wilkins responded, noting the point of such extreme hypotheticals is to test the governmentâs principles.

Christine Coogle of the Democracy Forward Foundation, representing the lawmakers, argued the case centered on whether lawmakers have the same entitlement to sue over the deprivation of information as private citizens when denied documents in a Freedom of Information case.

âThereâs no principle or case law that would suggest that Congress has less authority to provide that kind of entitlement when conferring it on its own members,â Coogle said, noting depriving members of information directly harms their oversight abilities.

Cobb ruled in December that an initial version of the policy violated a recurring provision in each congressional appropriations bill since 2020 that bars the department from using its appropriated funds to prevent lawmakers from conducting oversight visits or make any modifications that would hide conditions from lawmakers.

DHS then enacted a nearly identical policy on Jan. 8, which the government defended during a Jan. 14 hearing as drawing funds exclusively from the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, not the departmentâs annual appropriations. The Big Beautiful Bill appropriated $191 billion to DHS, as well as Congressâ short-term continuing resolution, which maintains 2025 appropriation levels through Jan. 30, 2026.

In her February ruling, Cobb rejected that representation after finding significant evidence the Jan. 8 policy was also âpromulgated, implemented and is presently being enforced with the use of Section 527 funds.â

Before the Jan. 14 hearing, Neguse informed Cobb that DHS blocked three members of Congress from conducting an oversight visit at an ICE facility in Minneapolis on Jan. 9, despite the Biden appointeeâs ruling.

Congressâ oversight power is a longstanding and central part of the legislative bodyâs purpose, and the Supreme Court has repeatedly upheld it as necessary for effective lawmaking. The representatives noted inÂ their July lawsuitÂ that the power is as âpenetrating and far-reachingâ as Congressâ appropriations powers, citing the 1959 caseÂ Barenblatt v. United States.

#7722. Justices to debate when an established rule is “previously unavailable” in habeas case

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

The Supreme Court will hear oral argument on Nov. 4 in Guerrero v. Johnson, a case about the limited circumstances in which a state prisoner can return to federal court for a second round of post-conviction review.

But let’s back up a bit: If inmates want to challenge the grounds for their detention, they must typically bring a habeas claim. The Antiterrorism and Effective Death Penalty Act of 1996, seeking to curb the number of such petitions, made it significantly more difficult to bring successive applications. Specifically, under 28 U.S.C. § 2244(b)(2) of AEDPA, a new claim in a second federal habeas petition is barred unless it falls under one of two exceptions. The first is when such a claim “relies on a new rule of constitutional law, made retroactive to cases on collateral review by the Supreme Court, that was previously unavailable.” The second exception covers claims based on “the facts underlying the [initial] claim,” but only if those facts would show “by clear and convincing evidence that, but for constitutional error, no reasonable factfinder would have found the applicant guilty of the underlying offense.”

Texas inmate Dexter Johnson brought his claim under the first exception, contending that he cannot be put to death based on the court’s 2002 ruling in Atkins v. Virginia, which held that executing people with intellectual disabilities violates the Eighth Amendment’s ban on cruel and unusual punishment. Johnson did not present the Atkins claim in his initial petitions but, after qualifying as intellectually disabled under revised diagnostic standards, raised this in a subsequent petition. The question before the justices is whether Johnson’s Atkins claim was “previously unavailable” to him.

In 2007, Johnson was convicted of capital murder and sentenced to death in Texas for his role in the double murder of 23-year-old Maria Aparece and 17-year-old Huy Ngo. At trial, a defense expert testified that Johnson’s IQ was between 74 and 88 and he “did not have obvious deficits” with regard to “personal independence and social responsibility when compared to other people of similar age and sociocultural background.” Under the diagnostic standards in place at that time, the expert concluded that Johnson was not intellectually disabled. (Johnson did not raise an Atkins claim in his initial habeas petitions but invoked Atkins in those petitions to argue – unsuccessfully – that its protections should extend to people with mental illness.)

In May 2013, while Johnson’s federal petition was pending, the American Psychiatric Association published the fifth edition of its diagnostic manual, known as the DSM-5, which Texas’ highest criminal court adopted in 2018. The new edition de-emphasized IQ cutoffs and recognized that someone whose score is above 70 may still be intellectually disabled. In April 2019, an expert gave Johnson an IQ test on which he scored 70, and a second expert agreed that Johnson met the DSM-5’s criteria for intellectual disability.

Johnson filed a successive habeas application in the district court, in which he claimed that he could not be executed under Atkins. After an evidentiary hearing, the trial court determined that Johnson’s Atkins claim was previously unavailable and consequently stayed his execution. The state appealed to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 5th Circuit, which in July 2025 affirmed the district court’s decision. The full 5th Circuit then declined to rehear the case by a vote of 9-7. In February, the state asked the Supreme Court to weigh in, which the Supreme Court agreed in June to do.

In its brief, the Office of the Texas Attorney General maintains that “Johnson’s Atkins claim does not rely on a change in the law.” Instead, it emphasizes, Atkins was decided well before Johnson filed his initial habeas application, and “before Johnson even committed the capital murder for which he was sentenced to death.” Nor, according to the Texas AG’s office, would permitting Johnson to bring such a claim serve the purpose of enabling successive petitions, which is to allow for new evidence as to whether a person is “guilty of the underlying offense.”

The state further presses the point that no “rule” was previously unavailable here. “An object—or a rule—can be available even when it is not needed or useful. A carpenter, for example, likely has a hammer ‘available,’ even when working on a task for which a hammer would not be necessary or useful,” the state writes. The publication of the DSM-5 may have allowed Johnson to discover a new factual predicate, according to the state, but it does not change the availability of any rule. Instead, the 5th Circuit’s approach “erases the line Congress drew between new law and new facts and effectively writes § 2244(b)(2)(B)’s limitations out of the statute.”

Johnson’s attorneys counter that something is “available” only if it is “capable of being used by a person, for a purpose”; prior to the publication of the DSM-5, no such usage was possible. “No one would say the hammer was available to the carpenter if it were locked in a toolbox he couldn’t open,” Johnson’s team writes. “Mr. Johnson did not change; his intellectual and adaptive characteristics are the same as always. What changed was the framework that made Atkins capable of protecting him. Atkins was not available to him before; now it is.” Nor, contrary to the AG’s claim otherwise, Johnson’s lawyers argue, would this open the “floodgates” to many other such challenges. Because very few rules are retroactive, such issues rarely arise.

Perhaps unsurprisingly given its stance on capital punishment, the Trump administration filed a “friend of the court” brief supporting Texas. Echoing several of the state’s arguments, U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer asserts that “[s]tandards promulgated by a board of psychiatrists cannot transform a decision of this Court that predates a prior habeas application into a ‘new’ and ‘previously unavailable’ rule of constitutional law.” Louisiana and 21 other states, also supporting Texas, call the 5th Circuit’s rule “a recipe for eternal Atkins claims and zero finality,” pointing out that a professional association also moved the age by which intellectual disability must appear from 18 to 22 in 2021 – raising the possibility that such age-based claims could also be brought and questioning the possibility that the habeas floodgates would remain closed were the court to agree with Johnson.

On Johnson’s side, the National Association of Criminal Defense Lawyers compares Johnson’s claim to second petitions based on new science about “microscopic hair comparison analysis, arson science, and shaken baby syndrome.” According to the NACDL, “claims of constitutional error grounded in faulty science in a second or successive petition” must be allowed to go forward because “flawed analytical methods may not be debunked until” it is too late.

One final thing worth mentioning: Last term, after hearing argument in Hamm v. Smith, a dispute over how courts should weigh multiple IQ scores in Atkins cases, the justices dismissed the case as improvidently granted (known as a “DIG”) – that is, they decided that it was a mistake to have agreed to hear the case in the first place and did not resolve it. At the end of his brief, Johnson asks the court to do the same in his case on the ground that the state has continually changed its arguments. Whatever the merits of Johnson’s position on that front, it seems unlikely the court will DIG two Atkins cases in successive terms.

The decision in Guerrero v. Johnson is expected by late June or early July.

Nora is an editorial assistant at SCOTUSblog, based in Washington, D.C.

Zach is the executive editor of SCOTUSblog.

#7721. What businesses should know about consent rules when calling consumers

Rules around obtaining consumer consent before calling or texting are in a state of legal and regulatory uncertainty – and companies should remain cautious.

Senosiain is an associate and Rollins is a shareholder at Gunster. Views are the authors’ own.

The Telephone Consumer Protection Act governs calls and text messages sent by businesses to consumers. One such rule is that businesses must obtain express written consent prior to sending text messages to consumers, if they are using an automated telephone dialing system or making calls using an artificial or pre-recorded voice, including the use of AI bots.

The TCPA also provides that businesses may not call or text consumers on the federal Do Not Call List unless prior express consent is given. Even basic telemarketing calls and text messages require prior express consent. Violation of the statute can trigger liability for up to $1,500 per call or text message sent.

Additionally, many states have their own version of the TCPA, deemed “mini-TCPAs,” that require compliance for all businesses who make calls to consumer-residents in that state, regardless of where the business is domiciled.

Many companies use lead generators which gather consumer consents for multiple businesses and then provide the companies with consent and contact information for those potential consumers. Lead generators who obtain proper written consent can be a very useful tool for companies. This was generally permissible under the TCPA.

However, in 2023, the Federal Communications Commission updated its TCPA rules requiring “one-to-one consent” which was to become effective Jan. 27, 2025.

The one-to-one consent rule provides that if a business uses an ATDS, artificial or prerecorded voice, the business must obtain prior express consent, one seller at a time.

Thus, it prevents lead generators from using a single consumer’s consent for multiple businesses. Additionally, the one-to-one consent rule provides that the consent must be clear and conspicuous, and the calls and texts initiated pursuant to the consent must be logically and topically associated with the interaction that prompted the consent. This rule applies to both text messages and phone calls.

On Jan. 24, 2025, the FCC postponed the 2023 order by a year, until Jan. 26, 2026. Later that same day the Eleventh Circuit Court of Appeals vacated the 2023 Order, thus eliminating the one-to-one consent rule.

The Eleventh Circuit Court of Appeals held “that the FCC exceeded its statutory authority under the TCPA because the 2023 Order’s new consent restrictions impermissibly conflict[ed] with the ordinary statutory meaning of prior express consent.”

Notably, the court ruled that the FCC exceeded its statutory authority at the outset, when it created the one-to-one consent rule. The court held that the 2023 Order’s one-to-one prior express consent restriction impermissibly conflicted with the ordinary statutory meaning of “prior express consent.” Thus, the Court vacated application of the 2023 Order, and remanded for further proceedings.

As a result, it is very likely that we will see other cases challenging TCPA regulations, especially as to the consent required before making a telemarketing call or text message using an ATDS.

It is unclear whether the FCC will revise its 2023 Order to comply with the Eleventh Circuit’s decision. In order to be prepared for this rule to come into effect, and in an abundance of caution, businesses who use lead generators to source potential consumers’ consent should ascertain that the lead generators are obtaining individual, one-to-one consent.

Businesses should also only contact consumers who provide this consent for telemarketing that is logically and topically associated with that which the consent was provided. Further, in addition to storing consumer contact information, businesses must retain the consent forms, information as to when consent was given, and through whom. Even businesses that do not use lead generators to obtain consent should continue to review their consent practices to ensure strict compliance with the TCPA and mini-TCPAs.

The TCPA requires prior express consent, and in many cases, prior express written consent, for calls and text messages made to prospective consumers. Regardless of any changes to the TCPA, the FTSA still requires that businesses obtain prior express written consent when making unsolicited telephone calls (including sending text messages) using an automated system. And lastly, to further protect your business, the consent form should have robust terms of service, including a class action waiver.

We continue to recommend that businesses ensure compliance with the TCPA, FTSA, and any other state regulations by always obtaining express written consent prior to contacting potential consumers via calls or text messages.

#7719. Lagunitas Brewing faces class action over claims of forever chemicals in beer

Plaintiff Nathaniel Talbot says testing shows Lagunitas beer contains levels of PFAS that are harmful to human health.

SAN FRANCISCO (CN) â A San Francisco man filed a class action against Lagunitas Brewing Company over claims its beers contain levels of perfluoroalkyl and polyfluoroalkyl chemicals, known as PFAS, that are harmful to human health.

Named plaintiff Nathaniel Talbot claims Lagunitas Brewing was or should have been aware of the levels of PFAS in its beer, and failed to warn customers of such levels.

âAt all relevant times and continuing to the present, defendant brewed, packaged, marketed, and sold the beer, in a uniform way that fails to disclose the fact that it contains levels of PFAS that the EPA has found pose health risks, which only defendant could and did know," Talbot says in his complaint, filed Monday in the Northern District of California.

Described as âforever chemicalsâ because they donât degrade naturally in the environment, PFAS â used in everything from firefighting foam to household items â have been linked to various health problems, including liver and immune-system damage and some cancers.

Talbot says he became concerned about the PFAS levels in Lagunitas beer following the release of an April 2025 study conducted by independent researchers looking into the association between PFAS in tap water and beer.

The study tested 23 beers brewed for 17 different PFAS from across the country, Talbot says. The study did not disclose which beers had been sampled, but âbeer 4â in the category of âbrewed in regions with PFAS in municipal drinking waterâ was identified as from Sonoma County, California, where Talbot says Lagunitas is the largest brewery and the only one that distributes its beer nationally and internationally.

Independent testing arranged by Talbot on four samples of Lagunitas beer from around the country found the beverages contained nearly seven times the EPAâs enforceable limit for perfluorooctanoic acid and about four times the EPAâs current enforceable limit for perfluorononanoic acid.

âPlaintiffâs testing was likely not the first finding that Lagunitas contained levels of PFAS that the EPA has found to pose a risk to human health, and accordingly the company was or should have been aware of the presence of PFAS in its beer,â Talbot said.

Talbot says he purchased and consumed Lagunitas beer regularly and claims he would not have bought the beer if he knew of the beverageâs health risks. However, he claims he would purchase Lagunitas again if the brewer could ensure its beer is free from PFAS.

âPlaintiff, a lifelong resident of Northern California, has an affection and fondness for Lagunitas beer as an iconic regional brand associated with positive local memories. He continues to desire to purchase it from defendant if he can rely on that beer to be free from PFAS, which are known to pose risks to human health,â he said.

Talbot brings claims of breach of the implied warranty and unfair competition, along with violations of the Consumers Legal Remedies Act and state unfair competition law.

A representative for Lagunitas did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

In a statement to Courthouse News, Carl L. Stine of Wolf Popper, representing Talbot, said it âappears that Lagunitas knowingly sells beer that contains levels of PFAS that the EPA has found to pose health risks.â

âWe believe Lagunitas should immediately fix this problem and pay damages to its customers, who unwittingly bought this flawed product,â he said.

Lagunitas Brewing Company was founded in 1993 in Lagunitas, California. It moved to nearby Petaluma two years later, where the company still operates and brews all its beer. The Dutch-based Heineken Company purchased a 50% stake in Lagunitas in 2015, opening the door to sell Lagunitas beer internationally. Heineken bought the remaining half of Lagunitas in 2017.

#7717. Conservative justices likely to endorse Catholic preschool exclusion of LGBTQ families

Colorado looked headed towards its fourth loss in row in Supreme Court matchups over LGBTQ rights and religious beliefs.

WASHINGTON (CN) â The Supreme Courtâs conservative supermajority seemed likely Tuesday to give anti-LGBTQ Catholic preschools a path around Coloradoâs requirement that taxpayer dollars only go to schools that are open to all.

During two hours of oral arguments, the Republican appointees dismissed Coloradoâs need to condition funding for its universal preschool program on an equal opportunity mandate, and they elevated concerns that nondiscrimination laws could be used to indirectly discriminate against religious beliefs.

âWhen a state imposes a condition that it knows certain religions cannot accept, the only question that is presented is whether that was done with the intent to discriminate against those religions,â Justice Samuel Alito, a George W. Bush appointee, said.

St. Mary Catholic Parish says it was excluded from the Centennial Stateâs universal preschool program because it is only open to families that are supportive of the Catholic Churchâs teaching on sex and marriage. The preschool filed a lawsuit in 2023 after being denied a religious exemption from Coloradoâs equal opportunity mandate.

Two lower courts dismissed the suit, finding Coloradoâs program did not explicitly discriminate based on religion. But the high court appeared likely to reverse, viewing the case in line with the Roberts courtâs recent First Amendment jurisprudence.

In Trinity Lutheran v. Comer in 2017, the court held churches couldnât be excluded from secular aid programs. Then, in 2020âs Espinoza v. Montana Department of Revenue, the justices ruled states couldnât refuse government aid to schools controlled by churches.

Those two rulings culminated in the Supreme Courtâs landmark 2022 ruling in Carson v. Makin, holding state-funded school choice programs must include education at religious institutions.

Chief Justice John Roberts, another George W. Bush appointee, said the effect of the law in Carson was the same in St. Maryâs case, preventing schools from receiving funding based on their religious beliefs.

Justice Amy Coney Barrett, a Donald Trump appointee, questioned why Colorado couldnât have foreseen its mandate being a problem when the high court has repeatedly ruled against the stateâs protections for LGBTQ rights in cases concerning cakemakers, website designers and conversion therapy.

Justice Neil Gorsuch, also a Trump appointee, further suggested states have intentionally enacted similar laws to Coloradoâs to circumvent the courtâs protections of religious beliefs.

The liberal wing had starkly different views on the case before the high court. All three Democratic appointees framed the matter as an attempt to greenlight discrimination against LGBTQ families.

âWhat you’re basically saying is we can exclude people merely because of exposure to them,â Justice Sonia Sotomayor, a Barack Obama appointee, said. âWe can exclude children of same-sex marriage. We can exclude children who might have transgender feelings or beliefs because exposing other children to them creates a problem.â

Sotomayor and the other liberal justices said excluding LGBTQ families was no different than using religious beliefs as justification for discriminating based on race.

âThere’s no principled basis, I think, to distinguish between an entity that says my religious faith says my children can’t go to school with the children of gay people from a religious entity that says my religion says my children can’t go to school with the children of Black people,â Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson, a Joe Biden appointee, said.

Instead of equal treatment, the liberal justices framed St. Maryâs case as a request for special treatment. As such, Justice Elena Kagan, another Obama appointee, said it was âfar-fetchedâ to suggest that Colorado was surreptitiously targeting religious beliefs.

St. Maryâs case asked the justices to apply strict scrutiny to public funding requirements that interfere with protected rights. But Kagan questioned why the high court would want to put itself in the middle of weighing the importance of religious beliefs versus nondiscrimination interests of the state in an endless number of cases.

The conservative justices appeared undeterred by their colleaguesâ concerns. Gorsuch remarked that he struggled to see how applying strict scrutiny would âbe the end of the world,âÂ and Justice Brett Kavanaugh, another Trump appointee, noted the courtâs support for LGBTQ rights wasnât in spite of other rights.

âOne of the things that Obergefell was very careful to say, though, was that in recognizing a constitutional right to same-sex marriage, that the court was also respecting the rights of people, particularly religious people, who had religious beliefs that were different, and that it was important going forward as a country to make sure both rights were respected,â Kavanaugh said.

#7716. Dems ask SEC, DOL to not issue anti-ESG rules: Exclusive

A coalition of 17 blue state finance officials sent a letter to the agencies to counter prior assertions made by their Republican colleagues.

The Democratic finance officials took particular issue with the Republican officials’ letter relying heavily on a federal judge’s ruling against American Airlines in a lawsuit over the management of its retirement plans. The Republican finance officials used U.S. District Court judge Reed O’Connor’s ruling as evidence that the incorporation of factors like ESG is being used to pursue non-pecuniary goals.

The officials included state auditors, treasurers, controllers and comptrollers from New York City, California, Illinois and 12 other states who said that such a characterization of the use of environmental, social and governance factors is “incorrect and dangerously misleading.”

“The decision in Spence v. American Airlines, which dismissed long-term financial interests as a ‘mere pretext,’ fails to reflect the fundamental reality of long-term investing,” the Democratic officials wrote. “Fiduciaries are not speculators — they are stewards of trillions of dollars in assets that must sustain retirees for decades.”

Officials from Connecticut, Colorado, Delaware, Maryland, Massachusetts, Minnesota, Nevada, New Mexico, Oregon, Rhode Island, Vermont and Washington also signed onto the letter. They said that risks related to climate change, governance failures and systemic issues are “present-day financial realities affecting market valuations, insurance costs, supply chains and infrastructure resilience."

The Republican officials had said in their Jan. 28 letter that they held “serious concerns” that funds were being used to advance ESG or DEI goals and asked for rulemaking to prohibit plans from using assets to “advance political or social goals.” They also asked the Labor Department and SEC to issue comprehensive guidance explicitly saying that making investment decisions or proxy votes based on ESG or diversity, equity and inclusion objectives is “inconsistent with fiduciary duties.”

Connecticut State Treasurer Erick Russell called the request a “dangerous political proposal” in emailed comments to ESG Dive Wednesday, while Illinois State Treasurer Michael Frerichs went a step further, calling the approach “Orwellian” and “a reckless attempt to put politics ahead of sound financial decision-making” in comments Wednesday.

“Forbidding investment managers from assessing real-world risks — whether they stem from supply chain disruptions, environmental instability, shifting consumer demand, or any other factor — would restrict their ability to fully analyze investment opportunities and inherently runs counter to that fiduciary responsibility,” Russell said.

The blue state fiduciaries warned that if utilizing ESG factors in investment decisions was banned for fiduciaries, it could cause weaker investment performance, create greater exposure to market volatility and increase financial vulnerability for retirees.

“As stewards of public funds, we have a responsibility to ensure that our investments provide stable, long-term returns over periods of decades,” Delaware State Treasurer Colleen Davis told ESG Dive. “It is morally reprehensible and financially negligent to play politics with the American people’s retirement savings and investments.”

Acting SEC Chair Mark Uyeda and Acting Labor Secretary Vince Micone are currently in charge of two agencies who are defending a pair of ESG-linked regulations in court. Uyeda said last week he would seek a delay in arguments in lawsuits about the SEC’s climate-risk disclosure rule, indicating the agency as constructed is not inclined to defend the rule. A federal judge recently ruled in favor of the Biden administration’s Labor Department on its regulation allowing fiduciaries to consider ESG and other collateral benefits in the case of a tiebreaker. Experts expect that both rules are endangered under this Trump administration.

#7713. A surge in cases on religion and schools

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

Welcome to a new month and a new argument session. The justices will hear argument in seven cases over the next nine days.

Today, the justices will hear argument in two cases: Maxwell v. Dinis, on a federal inmate’s ability to use a habeas statute, 28 U.S.C. § 2241, to contest the Federal Bureau of Prisons’ refusal to accelerate his transfer to a halfway house or home confinement; and Younge v. Fulton Judicial Circuit District Attorney’s Office, Georgia, on whether an affirmative defense may be asserted as a basis for summary judgment if not presented earlier in a pleading.

On Tuesday, the justices will hear argument in St. Mary Catholic Parish v. Roy, a religious discrimination challenge brought by Catholic preschools in Colorado over the state’s requirement that all schools participating in its universal preschool program must admit everyone – including LGBTQ children and children with LGBTQ parents.

On Oct. 21, the Trump administration asked the justices to allow it to resume construction of its border wall in the Big Bend region of southwestern Texas. The request is now fully briefed, and the court’s decision could come at any time.

#7712. Welsh council must take fresh look at homeowner’s cat feces complaint

In an email to his local council, the homeowner said he "wakes up with dread" every day thinking of the "cat mess" in his yard.

(CN) â A South Wales borough council cannot brush off a homeownerâs complaint about his neighborâs cats using his yard as a toilet just because felines have a âright to roam,â the U.K. Court of Appeal ruled Tuesday.

While refusing to make any final determination on the merits of the case, Lord Justice Robert Miles, writing for the three-justice panel, said âcat foulingâ can legally constitute a âdepositâ and a potential health nuisance under environmental law.

Cat fouling refers to a cat urinating or defecating outside its litter box or in unwanted outdoor areas â in this case, the front yard of a disgruntled neighbor.

Though the ruling stops short of turning outdoor cats into outlaws, it does mean councils can no longer shrug off nuisance complaints without proper investigation.

The dispute dates back to October 2024, when Richard Williamson, of Bedwas, Wales, complained to the Caerphilly County Borough Council that his neighborâs cats were repeatedly doing their business in his garden.

In an email to the council he sent alongside CCTV footage catching the felines in the act, Williamson said he âwakes up with dread each day wondering if there is yet more cat messâ in his yard â noting attempted resolutions with his neighbor proved fruitless.

While domestic cats, unlike dogs or livestock, have a legal âright to roamâ in the U.K., Williamson argued they do not have the right to cause a statutory nuisance â noting concerns about his familyâs newborn baby given the health risks associated with cat feces.

âThe cats are fouling on a weekly basis, and Iâm exhausted from repeatedly cleaning up after someone elseâs pets,â he added in an email to the council. âMy daughter should not be exposed to such dangers in her own home environment.â

The council investigated his claims, later dismissing the complaint, claiming that cats are generally allowed to move freely, that it was satisfied with how the cats were kept and that the animals had proper litter tray access.

An officer of the council further informed Williamson that cat owners are required to make âconsiderations of welfare,â noting owners not letting cats outside can be detrimental.

Last December, Judge Milwyn Jarman of the High Court of Justice quashed the councilâs decision and ordered it to redetermine Williamson’s complaint under the U.K. Environmental Protection Act â which covers statutory nuisances under distinct categories, including both how animals are kept and any âaccumulation or depositâ prejudicial to health.

âHad Parliament intended that section should not apply to cat feces left by roaming cats, it very easily could have made this an exception,â Jarman said in his December ruling. âThe cat feces in the present case were clearly capable of being prejudicial to health.â

Jarman ruled, and Miles affirmed, that borough councils cannot dismiss animal-related complaints purely under the âhow animals are keptâ rule, or rely on a general âright to roamâ without independently investigating whether physical deposits, like cat fouling, constitute a health hazard or nuisance.

The appeal court rejected the councilâs argument that, for something to qualify as a âdepositâ under the act, the item must have been placed by a purposeful or willful act â ruling deposit alone refers to the physical existence of a substance, regardless of how it got there.

âThis is all about the physical world and has nothing to do with anybodyâs actions or responsibility,â Miles wrote in the order. âThe duties of inspection and investigation are concerned with whether there is a statutory nuisance falling within the subsection, not with who has caused or suffered it to happen.â

While the council cautioned the court that a ruling against it could have âprofound consequences for cat owners and local authorities,â Miles clarified the ruling simply orders a redetermination of Williamsonâs complaint.

âIt emphatically does not decide that the cat fouling about which the respondent has complained constitutes a statutory nuisance,â he said in the order.

Neither party’s attorneys responded to initial requests for comment.

Lord Justice Christopher Nugee and Lord Justice Stephen Males rounded out the panel.

#7709. Lindsay Clancy judge considers retrial at hearing to dismiss murder case

Lindsay Clancy was being tried for first-degree murder. She admitted to killing her three children and claimed that she suffered from postpartum psychosis. (Photo by CJ Gunther/The Boston Herald via the Associated Press)

The possible retrial date for Lindsay Clancy, a former labor and delivery nurse charged with strangling and killing her three small children in 2023, might be March 2027, according to a Massachusetts judge during a Monday hearing to determine whether the triple murder case should be dismissed.

Massachusetts Superior Court Judge William Sullivan offered the tentative retrial date, and prosecutors in the case said they fully intend to retry Clancy, 36, who admitted to strangling to death her three children—5-year-old daughter Cora; 3-year-old son Dawson; and 8-month-old son Callan—during a postpartum psychosis episode. She later cut her wrists and neck and jumped from a second-story window, which paralyzed her from the waist down, according to coverage by Courthouse News Service.

The five-week trial resulted in a jury deadlock after one juror held out to convict Clancy. Eleven jurors were prepared to present a not guilty by reason of insanity verdict, which would have sent Clancy to a psychiatric facility instead of sentencing her to life in prison.

Michael Desronvil, the lone dissenter, wanted to convict and faced scrutiny after his name was leaked on the internet.

Jennifer Sprague, a Plymouth County, Massachusetts, assistant district attorney, defended Desronvil’s decision but did not comment on what charges that Clancy would face in a new trial.

#7705. DOJ sends election monitors to all 50 states amid midterm election voting

The 1,000 monitors have largely been sent to jurisdictions that voted for Kamala Harris in 2024 and are populated by Black and Latino voters; Michigan and Texas have the most jurisdictions listed.

WASHINGTON (CN) â The Justice Department announced Tuesday that it had, for the first time in American history, deployed over 1,000 election monitors to polling stations in all 50 states.

The announcement comes after a highly polarized campaign for the November midterms that is likely to shake up the power balance in Washington against President Donald Trump, as he faces historically low approval ratings over his handling of the economy, his extreme anti-immigrant agenda and his unpopular war in Iran.

Throughout the 50 states, the monitors have been sent to certain jurisdictions in each state. Of the 126 jurisdictions, former Vice President Kamala Harris defeated President Donald Trump in about two-thirds of the locations in the 2024 presidential election.

Michigan and Texas â the two states with the most highlighted Senate races in the country this midterm cycle, between Democrat Abdul El-Sayed and Republican Mike Rogers in Michigan and Democrat James Talarico and Republican Ken Paxton in Texas â have the most listed jurisdictions, with seven and eight, respectively.

New York, Illinois and Georgia each had five jurisdictions listed, while Florida, California, Arizona, Pennsylvania and Virginia had four. Black and Latino voters make up a majority in many of the 126 jurisdictions.

According to the Justice Department, the Civil Rights Division is leading the effort, with personnel from the division, other Justice Department components, U.S. attorneysâ offices and federal observers from the Office of Personnel Management.

Assistant Attorney General Harmeet K. Dhillon, head of the Civil Rights Division, announced the monitorsâ deployment as a continuation of the Justice Departmentâs long-standing practice of sending monitors under the 1965 Voting Rights Act.

âElection integrity has been one of the top priorities for this administration and this Division,â Dhillon said in a statement. âI am very proud we are deploying the largest monitoring effort in DOJ history, and pursuing transparency for elections in an assertive and nondiscriminatory manner.â

Trump has spent a large part of the last year reviving claims of election fraud, both in his previous electoral losses and in advance of the November midterms, and instructing the Justice Department to pursue an unprecedented litigation campaign against states to purge their voter rolls of supposed noncitizens.

In a July national address, Trump rehashed claims of foreign interference in the 2020 presidential election, asserting China carried out âthe largest compromise of election data in historyâ by acquiring 220 million U.S. voter files.

This past week, Trump urged the Supreme Court to set aside 20,000 ballots from suspected noncitizens in California, marking a major escalation in the administrationâs effort to exert federal control in state-run elections. The Justice Department filed a similar challenge in Washington state, where it advanced further claims of noncitizen voter fraud.

The justices swiftly rejected the request on Monday, denying the governmentâs emergency request before hearing any briefing from California officials in an unsigned order without any noted dissents.

In another unprecedented case, the Justice Department sued to block the certification of election results in Alaskaâs Senate race over concerns voters will be confused by the inclusion of two Dan Sullivans on the ballot. Incumbent Republican Senator Dan Sullivan faces Democrat Representative Mary Peltola, as well as Daniel Sullivan Jr., who is not affiliated with a political party.

On Sunday, U.S. District Judge Sharon Gleason found the Justice Departmentâs request would violate Alaskan votersâ right to a secret ballot.

Throughout the country, the Trump administration has also sought to create a national voter database by demanding states hand over their voter rolls, which it argued would allow it to remove any noncitizens and prevent them from voting Tuesday.

Voting rights organizations sued in Washington, citing several examples of U.S. citizens in red states who complied with such demands having their voter registrations canceled erroneously.

The rolls include sensitive personal data such as home addresses, Social Security numbers and voting history. As a result, while at least 18 states have fully cooperated with the Justice Departmentâs demands, 26 states have refused.

Thatâs led the Justice Department to sue in efforts to compel the states to produce their voter rolls. In all 26 of those states, federal judges have dismissed the Justice Departmentâs lawsuits after ruling the efforts unlawful. Additionally, the Sixth Circuit has also upheld the dismissal of one such lawsuit.

U.S. District Judge Sparkle Sooknanan, a Joe Biden appointee, ruled on Oct. 9 that the Justice Department could not use the flawed database to revoke any U.S. citizenâs voter registration, slamming it as a clear effort to âdecide who gets to vote.â

#7704. Justice Kagan: firing point blank in Smith & Wesson v. Estados Unidos Mexicanos

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

In the 1983 movie A Christmas Story, Ralphie’s teacher, Miss Shields, assigns her students the task of writing “a theme.” The fourth-grade class at Warren G. Harding Elementary school erupts in groans; after all, writing is hard work.

But Ralphie sees it as an opportunity to make his case for a Red Ryder BB gun, “the Holy Grail of Christmas gifts.” And as the words “pour[] forth from [his] penny pencil with feverish fluidity,” he gets right to the point: “What I want for Christmas is a Red Ryder BB gun with a compass in the stock and this thing that tells time.”

Doubtless, Miss Shields had admonished her students – like our teachers admonished us – that each paragraph of a theme must begin with a thesis (or topic) sentence. But is that always right? Pay attention to skilled writers, and you’ll discover that – like many things – it depends.

Skilled writers do locate a paragraph’s issue (topic) and its point (thesis) where readers expect to encounter them. But readers have different expectations about where that should be. Sometimes readers expect the issue and the point in the first sentence, but sometimes they expect them to be separated. Readers change their expectations depending on what type of paragraph they are reading. And sometimes a paragraph has no point at all.

Justice Elena Kagan shows how this works. She never makes a reader hunt for her point, even though she might locate that point in different places for different types of paragraphs.

Take Smith & Wesson v. Estados Unidos Mexicanos as one of many potential examples. In Smith & Wesson, the court held that Mexico had failed to plead its way around a federal statute barring claims against gun manufacturers. Starting with meat-and-potatoes paragraphs, Kagan does exactly what Miss Shields might insist upon. She locates both the issue and the point of the paragraph right at the beginning, then uses the rest of the paragraph to prove her point.

In Section I.A. of the opinion, for example, Kagan sets out the requirements of the statute being interpreted, the Protection of Lawful Commerce in Arms Act. Taking only the first sentence of each paragraph, readers learn exactly how the statute works with zero effort. We read:

“[The PLCAA] bars cer­tain lawsuits against manufacturers and sellers of fire­arms.”

“But PLCAA’s general bar on those suits has an exception, usually called the predicate exception, relevant here.”

“Notably here, the predicate violation PLCAA demands may come from aiding and abetting someone else’s firearms offense.”

After each thesis, Kagan deploys the PLCAA’s language to prove that she’s right. For example, to prove that the PLCAA “bars certain lawsuits,” she quotes language providing that a “qualified civil liability action . . . may not be brought in any Federal or State court.” But again, before she shoves the reader’s nose into the language, she first tells us the point of it all.

In adopting this structure, Kagan is giving English readers what they expect. In his book “The Sense of Structure,” George Gopen calls these meat-and-potatoes paragraphs “medial paragraphs.” Here, in the middle of an exposition, “readers tend to appreciate being given the point up front.” Fail to put the point up front and one risks “having the reader disappear before the point actually arrives.” You run an especially grave risk if you are writing for busy legal readers – an audience that’s typically looking for a reason to stop reading.

But in other types of paragraphs, Kagan does not front-load a traditional thesis sentence, and she’s right there too. Consider the way Kagan writes introductions and narrative paragraphs.

In her Smith & Wesson introduction, Kagan reveals the issue or the topic in the first sentence, but she only gives the point or thesis in the last sentence. In the first sentence, we read that Mexico has sued American gun manufacturers – what the case is about. But before we can understand the court’s holding – the point – we need to learn some context. We need a sketch of what the law requires. So Kagan next sets out the statutory requirement: Mexico must plead that the gun manufacturers aided and abetted unlawful sales to the cartels. Only now, at the end of the paragraph, do we know enough to understand the point: Mexico did not plausibly plead aiding and abetting.

Again, according to Gopen, Kagan is satisfying her readers’ “remarkably fixed expectation that the point of an opening paragraph will arrive at the end.” We readers don’t want to be punched in the face with an answer before we know enough to understand it. Writers should make us “comfortable with the surroundings before we have to go to work.”

Narrative paragraphs involve yet another difference: readers don’t expect a traditional thesis in a passage that feels like “once upon a time.” Gopen notes, “Not all paragraphs were born to make a point.” Sometimes writers write “just to tell a story, to put some facts on the table.”

In her narrative paragraphs, Kagan sometimes just tells the story, and sometimes she fires a thesis point blank:

In the end, your old English teacher was mostly right. Ordinary, meat-and-potatoes paragraphs ought to have a sentence in which the issue and the point are together at the beginning of the paragraph. But specialized paragraphs might be different. So, before you start line-editing the sentences of a draft, employ a process to evaluate the strength of your paragraphs.

For your meat-and-potatoes paragraphs, prefer paragraphs that state the point and then prove it. Be on the lookout for paragraphs that write to a conclusion rather than stating it up front. To diagnose these paragraphs, try to create a reverse outline by copying the first sentence (sometimes two) into a different document. Ask yourself whether the argument makes sense with only those sentences. It will if the issue and point are stated up front.

In your statement of facts, mark which paragraphs have a thesis and which don’t. Know that you have a choice about when to include one, and make that choice.

Finally, give special attention to paragraphs that begin a text or a new section. Take the reader from the issue, through the necessary context, and then conclude with the point.

Why so much care? Because hitting the wrong target can be dangerous; you’ll shoot your eye out. A legal reader won’t just stand by trying to guess where the next round is being aimed.

Correction (Nov. 2 at 5:00 p.m.): A prior version of this article gave the case name as Smith & Wesson v. Estados Unidos de Mexico.

Professor Gray teaches legal writing courses for first-year and advanced students at Duke Law.
